K-317.h1: Letter of the Week: Trace, Circle and Write One Letter
K-317.title: Letter of the Week Worksheet for Kindergarten | Free Printable PDF
K-317.metaDescription: Letter of the week worksheet: trace the big and small letter, circle the four pictures that begin with it, then write a row of each. Free printable Kindergarten PDF.
K-317.p1: One letter fills this Kindergarten letter-of-the-week worksheet from top to bottom, and the page shown here is the Mm sheet. A cream card at the top left prints the capital and small letter on handwriting lines; beside it run two tracing lanes, one for M and one for m, each starting with a solid model letter and continuing in dashed letters with red stroke dots and arrows on the first. Below the lanes sit eight picture cards in two rows of four — on this sheet a mountain, a nut, a wallet, a monkey, a mouse, a net, a mop and a nurse — and the child circles the four whose name begins with the letter. Two full-width handwriting rows at the bottom, one headed M and one headed m, are for writing a row of each letter alone.
K-317.p2: The sheet does the three jobs a letter introduction needs in the order a classroom does them: the shape first, then the sound, then the letter written without a guide. The four foil pictures are chosen so that none begins with the target — several on the M sheet begin with n, which looks and sounds close — so the child has to say each word and listen to its first sound rather than recognize a shape. Nothing on the page is labeled; the picture names stay in the child's mouth.
K-317.p3: It prints on one sheet in portrait and needs only a pencil. The words-with page in this family moves the letter away from the start of the word, the beginning-middle-end page asks where the sound sits, and the M-or-N page puts two look-alike letters side by side.

K-325.h1: Words with the Letter: Hear It Anywhere in the Word
K-325.title: Words with the Letter Worksheet for Kindergarten | Free Printable PDF
K-325.metaDescription: Words-with worksheet: trace the letter, then circle the four pictures that have its sound somewhere inside the word, not at the start. Free printable Kindergarten PDF.
K-325.p1: Instead of asking which word begins with the letter, this Kindergarten words-with page asks where else the letter hides. The Mm version shown here keeps the letter card and the two tracing lanes of the letter-of-the-week base at the top, then lays out eight picture cards — a jar of jam, a lamp, a net, a camel, a window, a necklace, a watch and a hammer — and the child circles the four that have the M sound somewhere inside the word but not at the start: jam, lamp, camel and hammer. The two handwriting rows for M and m close the page as before.
K-325.p2: Hearing a sound in the middle or at the end of a word is a later skill than hearing it first, because the child has to hold the whole word and scan it. The shipped configuration guarantees that at least two of the four hits carry the letter in the middle of the word rather than at the end, so the page cannot be solved by listening for a final sound alone. The four foils never begin with the target letter either, which removes the shortcut of circling anything that starts with it — that is the base page's job, not this one's.
K-325.p3: Print it after the base sheet for the same letter, once the child can find the letter at the start without hesitating. The trace lanes and write rows mean it still counts as a handwriting page, so it fits the same letter-of-the-week slot in a weekly plan. The beginning-middle-end page is the natural next step: it takes the same idea and asks the child to say which of the three positions the sound is in.

K-326.h1: Beginning, Middle or End: Where Is the Letter?
K-326.title: Beginning, Middle or End Worksheet for Kindergarten | Free Printable PDF
K-326.metaDescription: Beginning, middle or end worksheet: say each of six picture words and color the box that shows where the letter is heard in the word. Free printable Kindergarten PDF.
K-326.p1: Six wide cards, two across and three down, make up this Kindergarten beginning-middle-end page for one letter of the week — the sheet shown is for M. Each card carries a color picture, the word printed on a handwriting rule beside it (tomato, lamp, mailbox, mountain, worm, broom), and under the word three dashed boxes. A tiny key sits above the boxes: three small squares with the first, the middle or the last square shaded, one key per box. The child says the word, decides whether the M is heard at the beginning, in the middle or at the end, and colors that box. A slim strip at the top holds the letter card and a single lane of dashed capital letters to trace; there are no write rows on this face.
K-326.p2: The page is built so that every position is represented: two of the six words carry the letter at the beginning, two in the middle and two at the end. That balance stops a child from coloring the first box every time and being right often enough to keep doing it. Printing the word next to the picture is deliberate at this level — a child who has just met the letter can check the sound against the letter they can see, which is the bridge between phonemic awareness and phonics that this task sits on.
K-326.p3: Coloring rather than writing keeps the page short; most children finish it in a few minutes, so it works as a warm-up before the base letter sheet or as a quick check afterward. It uses the same letter fan as the rest of the letter-of-the-week family, so a set for the week can be printed together. For the version where the letter is counted inside words rather than located, see the circle-and-count page.

K-327.h1: Circle the Letter in the Words and Count
K-327.title: Circle the Letter and Count Worksheet for Kindergarten | Free Printable PDF
K-327.metaDescription: Circle and count worksheet: find every big or small letter in six picture words, circle each one, then write how many in the box. Free printable Kindergarten PDF.
K-327.p1: Six long rows run down this Kindergarten circle-and-count page, each with a small picture at the left, its word printed large on a handwriting rule, and a dashed box at the right end. The sheet shown is the M version: mask, mitten, HAMMER, MONKEY, arm and mushroom. Two of the six words are printed in capitals and four in small letters, so the child is hunting for both M and m. In each word the child circles every letter of the week and writes the count in the box — one in most rows here, two in hammer and mushroom. The top of the page carries the letter card and one lane of dashed capitals to trace, and nothing else.
K-327.p2: Where the base page asks the child to hear a sound, this one asks them to see a letter, in both cases, anywhere in a word — the visual side of knowing a letter. Some words hold the letter once and some twice, and the shipped configuration keeps at least eight letters to find across the six rows, so the count is never all ones. Reading the word aloud is not required, but the picture invites it, and a teacher can listen for whether the child says the letter's sound as they circle.
K-327.p3: Print one per child; the rows are wide enough for a crayon circle and the count box takes a single numeral. Because it carries a tracing lane, it still gives a minute of handwriting on the letter. Pair it with the beginning-middle-end page, which uses the same six-card layout but asks about the sound's position instead of its count.

G1-311.h1: Sound of the Week: Trace the Digraph and Circle the Pictures
G1-311.title: Sound of the Week Worksheet for 1st Grade | Free Printable PDF
G1-311.metaDescription: Sound of the week worksheet: trace a two-letter sound such as sh, circle the four pictures that have it in the word, then write a row. Free printable 1st grade PDF.
G1-311.p1: Two letters that make one sound take the place of the single letter on this 1st grade sound-of-the-week page. The sheet shown is sh: a card at the top left prints Sh on handwriting lines, two tracing lanes carry Sh and sh as a solid model followed by dashed copies with stroke dots, and below them sit eight picture cards — a hamster, a ghost, a horse, a shovel, a shoe, a radish, a whisk and a starfish. The child circles the four that have the sh sound anywhere in the word: shovel, shoe, radish and starfish. Two handwriting rows at the bottom, headed Sh and sh, are for writing the digraph unaided.
G1-311.p2: The foils are the point of this page. Every wrong picture contains an s or an h somewhere — hamster, ghost, horse, whisk — without ever containing the sh sound, so a child who circles anything with an s in it is caught, and a child who listens for the single blended sound is not. Hits may carry the sound at the start or the end of the word, which is why radish and starfish sit beside shoe and shovel. The English set runs over sh, ch and th, each on its own sheet.
G1-311.p3: Print it once single-letter sheets are routine and the class is meeting digraphs; the layout is identical to the letter-of-the-week base, so the child already knows what to do. It carries no letter-name task, only the sound, and pairs with sound boxes pages where a wide box holds the same two letters. The digraph sheets of this family all print on one portrait page.

K-328.h1: M or N? Hear the Difference at the Start of the Word
K-328.title: M or N Worksheet for Kindergarten | Free Printable PDF
K-328.metaDescription: M or n worksheet: say each of eight picture words and circle the letter it begins with, m or n, on the two chips under the picture. Free printable Kindergarten PDF.
K-328.p1: Two easily confused letters share this Kindergarten m-or-n page. Eight picture cards in two rows of four fill the lower two thirds of the sheet — a nest, a necklace, a moon, a nose, a medal, a bottle of milk, a nurse and a mitten — and under every picture sit two small chips, one printed m and one printed n. The child says the word and circles the chip for the sound it begins with. The four m words and four n words are shuffled across the grid. Above the cards, a slim strip holds the Mm letter card and a single lane of dashed capital M to trace.
K-328.p2: M and n are neighbors in the mouth as well as in the alphabet, and children who have learned each letter on its own sheet still mix them up when the two are offered together. This face makes the choice explicit and binary: every card is one or the other, nothing else, so the page measures the one discrimination and not letter knowledge in general. Saying the word with the hand on the lips — m closes them, n does not — is the classroom cue that turns the page into a lesson.
K-328.p3: The chip layout takes a crayon or pencil circle and prints on one sheet. Use it after both letters have had their own week, not as an introduction to either. The English version pairs m with n; other minimal pairs in the family follow the same eight-card shape. The base letter-of-the-week sheet for M or N is the page to print first.

K-318.h1: Sound Boxes with Animals: One Sound in Each Box
K-318.title: Sound Boxes Worksheet with Animals for Kindergarten | Free Printable PDF
K-318.metaDescription: Sound boxes worksheet: say six animal words slowly and write one sound in each dashed box; a wide box with a curve holds two letters for one sound. Free printable K PDF.
K-318.p1: Six numbered cards, two across and three down, make up this Kindergarten sound boxes worksheet with animals. Each card shows one large color picture — on this sheet a cat, a donkey, a koala, a camel, a panda and a tiger — and under it a row of empty dashed boxes, one for every sound in the word: three for cat, four for tiger, five for the others. Where two letters spell one sound, the box is wider and has a small curve drawn beneath it, as in the ey of donkey and the er of tiger. No letters of the word are printed anywhere on the page; the child says the word slowly, listens, and writes one sound into each box in order.
K-318.p2: This is the Elkonin box task: the boxes tell the child how many sounds to listen for, and the wide box tells them where a sound will need two letters. That scaffold is what separates it from a plain spelling test — the structure is given, the letters are not. Words run from three to five sounds at this level, and the theme word bank keeps the pictures nameable by a five-year-old. Watch for a child writing a letter per box by sight; the page only works if the word is said aloud first.
K-318.p3: Print one per child, or one for a small group with a whiteboard beside it for the say-it-slowly step. The count-the-sounds page removes the boxes altogether, and the first-sound-given page writes the first letter in for the child.

K-329.h1: Count the Sounds: One Dot for Every Sound You Hear
K-329.title: Count the Sounds Worksheet for Kindergarten | Free Printable PDF
K-329.metaDescription: Count the sounds worksheet: say six household words slowly, draw one dot in the long box for every sound, then write the number. Free printable Kindergarten PDF.
K-329.p1: No letters and no separate boxes: this Kindergarten count-the-sounds page gives each of its six around-the-house pictures one long dashed box and one small square. The sheet shown has a mirror, a kitchen, a shovel, a spoon, a bowl and a rug. The child says the word slowly, draws one dot in the long box for every sound heard, then counts the dots and writes the numeral in the small box. Words on this face hold between two and five sounds, so the answer is a small number and the dots stay readable.
K-329.p2: Because the long box gives no hint of how many sounds to expect, this is a harder listening task than the base sound boxes page even though nothing is written but dots and a numeral. It is also a purer one: a child who cannot yet form letters can still show that they hear four sounds in spoon and three in rug. Watch how the dots are spaced — a child who draws one dot per letter or per syllable is showing where their segmenting still needs work.
K-329.p3: It prints on one sheet and needs a pencil or a crayon. Use it before the base sound boxes page as a listening-only warm-up, or afterward to check that the counting survives without the boxes. The sound strip page for 1st grade returns to boxes but hides the count in the same way. Other household themes print with the same layout.

K-330.h1: Sound Boxes with the First Sound Given: Finish the Word
K-330.title: First Sound Given Sound Boxes for Kindergarten | Free Printable PDF
K-330.metaDescription: First sound given worksheet: the first letter of each clothing word is printed; say the word slowly and fill every empty sound box. Free printable Kindergarten PDF.
K-330.p1: Every word on this Kindergarten sound boxes page starts for the child: the first box is already filled in, and the rest are empty. Six clothing pictures sit on numbered cards, two across and three down — on this sheet a vest, a pair of jeans, a scarf, a blouse, a beanie and a pair of boots — with four or five dashed boxes under each, the first letter printed in teal (v, j, s, b, b, b). Wide boxes with a curve beneath mark the two-letter sounds: the ea of jeans, the ar of scarf, the oo of boots, two in blouse and two in beanie. The child says the word slowly and writes one sound in each empty box.
K-330.p2: Giving the first sound solves the part of the task that a hesitant child gets stuck on — starting — and leaves the middle and end sounds, which are the ones that matter for segmenting. Words on this face are longer than the base page's, four to five sounds each, so the scaffold buys a step up in length rather than a step down in difficulty. Three of the six on this sheet begin with b, which is fine: the printed letter is a starting point, not a clue to sort by.
K-330.p3: Print it for children who finished the base sound boxes page with help, or as the middle step between counting sounds and writing them all. The wide boxes matter more here than on the base, so it is worth saying beforehand that the curve means two letters, one sound. Other clothing and non-clothing themes print in the same six-card layout.

G1-312.h1: Sound Strip: How Many Sounds in the Word?
G1-312.title: Sound Strip Worksheet with Zoo Animals for 1st Grade | Free Printable PDF
G1-312.metaDescription: Sound strip worksheet: six zoo animal words, six identical boxes each; write one sound per box from the left and leave the rest empty. Free printable 1st grade PDF.
G1-312.p1: Six identical dashed boxes follow every picture on this 1st grade sound strip page, whatever the word. The sheet shown runs six zoo animals down the page in single rows — a panda, a koala, a bison, a zebra, a tiger and a seal — each with the same strip of six squares beside it. The child says the word slowly and writes one sound in each box starting at the left, then stops; the boxes not needed stay empty. Nothing marks a wide box and nothing tells the child how many sounds to expect. Words on this face run from three to six sounds.
G1-312.p2: The fixed strip is what makes this a 1st grade page. In the Kindergarten sound boxes the number of boxes is the answer to how many sounds; here the strip is the same for seal and for zebra, so the child has to decide the count alone and write a two-letter sound into a single box without a wide-box hint. That is the segmenting skill without its scaffold, the step just before spelling from dictation. A quick glance down the right-hand side shows a teacher at once who over-segments and who stops early.
G1-312.p3: Print it once the base sound boxes page is easy; the layout is plain enough to reuse weekly with a new zoo animals draw or another theme. It pairs with the syllables-and-sounds page, which puts the arcs and box counts back but for longer words. One portrait sheet, pencil only.

G1-313.h1: Syllables and Sounds: Clap, Then Write One Sound in Each Box
G1-313.title: Syllables and Sounds Worksheet for 1st Grade | Free Printable PDF
G1-313.metaDescription: Syllables and sounds worksheet: clap each two- or three-syllable household word, then write one sound in each box under its syllable arc. Free printable 1st grade PDF.
G1-313.p1: Arcs are printed above the boxes on this 1st grade syllables-and-sounds page, one arc per syllable, with a gap between the syllable groups. Six around-the-house pictures run down the sheet in single rows — a window, a bottle of shampoo, a closet, a curtain, a mailbox and a toolbox — and each word's boxes are split under two arcs on this sheet, three boxes then two for window, three then three for mailbox. Wide boxes with a curve beneath mark two-letter sounds. The child claps the syllables, then says each syllable slowly and writes one sound in each box under its arc. The whole word is never printed.
G1-313.p2: Longer words defeat one-pass segmenting, and syllables are how readers get through them: clap the word into parts, then hear the sounds inside each part. The two-tier layout builds exactly that habit, with words of four to seven sounds across two or three syllables on this face. It stays a sound boxes page rather than a syllable-division page because the letters are the task — the arcs are given, the syllable count is given, and what the child produces is the spelling of each part.
G1-313.p3: Print it after the six-box sound strip page, when a child can segment a one-syllable word without help. Saying the word with a clap per syllable before writing is worth modeling on the first row. A window, a closet and a mailbox are all on this sheet, so the around-the-house theme also feeds classroom vocabulary; other themes print with the same arcs.

G1-314.h1: Blend the Sounds: Read the Boxes, Circle the Picture
G1-314.title: Blend the Sounds Worksheet with Toys for 1st Grade | Free Printable PDF
G1-314.metaDescription: Blend the sounds worksheet: the sounds of a toy word are printed one per box; read them, blend the word and circle its picture out of three. Free printable G1 PDF.
G1-314.p1: The boxes are already filled on this 1st grade blend-the-sounds page — the child reads instead of writes. Six rows carry a word from the toys theme printed one sound per dashed box at the left (on this sheet g-ir-l, l-e-g-o, sh-o-v-e-l, b-a-ll, d-o-ll, b-u-ck-e-t, with a curve under each two-letter box) and three small pictures at the right, one of which matches. The child says the sounds in order, blends them into the word, and circles the picture that names it: the ball rather than the truck or the kite, the bucket rather than the rocket or the sandbox. Words run from three to five sounds, with at most one wide box each.
G1-314.p2: This is the base sound boxes page run backward, and the reversal is what it teaches. Segmenting is hearing the sounds in a word; blending is pushing printed sounds back together into one, and children who can do one are not always able to do the other. Two of the three pictures share the theme with the answer but not its sounds, so the choice cannot be made from the picture alone; it has to come from the reading. The wide boxes with their curve show the child where a digraph is read as a single sound.
G1-314.p3: Print it as the reading counterpart to the segmenting pages: base sound boxes on Monday, blend the sounds on Tuesday, with the same theme. Toys are on this sheet; other themes use the same six-row layout. One portrait page, a pencil or crayon, no writing required.

G1-305.h1: Syllable Division with Animals: Draw a Scoop Under Every Syllable
G1-305.title: Syllable Division Worksheet with Animals for 1st Grade | Free Printable PDF
G1-305.metaDescription: Syllable division worksheet: six animal words printed in full; say each one, clap its parts and draw one scoop under every syllable. Free printable 1st grade PDF.
G1-305.p1: The whole word is printed on this 1st grade syllable division worksheet with animals — the child shows where it breaks. Six numbered cards, two across and three down, each hold a large color picture with its word spelled out in spaced letters below and a thin line under the word; on this sheet the words are woodpecker, elephant, vulture, donkey, reindeer and seagull. The child says the word, claps its parts, and draws one scoop — a small curved arc — under each syllable along that line. Words of two and three syllables are mixed, with at least two three-syllable words on every sheet at this level, and up to eleven letters.
G1-305.p2: Drawing the scoops is the syllable task in its purest form: nothing is counted into a box and no syllable is written, so the only thing the child produces is the division itself, and a teacher can see at a glance whether woodpecker got three arcs or two. Multisyllable animal names give the practice a reason, because these are the words a first grader meets in a nonfiction book and stalls on. The letters are spaced so that an arc can be drawn cleanly under each part.
G1-305.p3: It prints on one sheet and needs a pencil. The write-the-word-in-syllables page has the child copy the word with dashes instead of drawing arcs, and the two-or-three page sorts a word bank by syllable count.

G1-325.h1: Write the Word in Syllables: Copy It with a Dash at Every Break
G1-325.title: Write the Word in Syllables Worksheet for 1st Grade | Free Printable PDF
G1-325.metaDescription: Write the word in syllables: read six printed zoo animal words, copy each on the line and write a small dash between its syllables. Free printable 1st grade PDF.
G1-325.p1: Copying is the mechanism on this 1st grade write-the-word-in-syllables page. Six rows run down the sheet, each with a small zoo animals picture at the left, the word printed in bold beside it, and a three-line handwriting rule filling the right half. The words on this sheet are chimpanzee, elephant, meerkat, panda, cheetah and hyena. The child reads the printed word, says it in parts, and writes it on the rule with a small dash at every syllable break — chim-pan-zee, meer-kat (not mee-rkat). Words run to twelve letters and two or three syllables, with at least two of the longer three-syllable words on every sheet.
G1-325.p2: Where the base syllable division page has the child mark the breaks on a printed word, this face has them produce the word themselves, break by break. Handwriting and syllable division are combined on purpose: writing a word in chunks is how a first grader is taught to spell a long one, and the dash makes each chunk a decision. Because the model is printed, spelling is not the test; a child who copies the letters right but dashes in the wrong place has shown the teacher exactly which skill needs work.
G1-325.p3: Print one per child; the rule gives room for a large hand. Use it after the scoop page, when the breaks are heard reliably and the goal is to carry them into writing. The missing-syllable page is the next step, where one part of the word is gone and must be supplied.

G1-326.h1: Missing Syllable: Say the Picture, Write the Part That Is Gone
G1-326.title: Missing Syllable Worksheet for 1st Grade | Free Printable PDF
G1-326.metaDescription: Missing syllable worksheet: eight household picture words each have one syllable replaced by a box; say the word and write the missing part. Free printable 1st grade PDF.
G1-326.p1: Half of every word is on the page and half is not. This 1st grade missing-syllable worksheet lays out eight cards in two columns of four, each with an around-the-house picture — a hammer, a wall outlet, a mailbox, a closet, scissors, curtains, a mirror and a window on this sheet — and beneath it the word in spaced letters with one syllable replaced by a dashed box: ham ___, ___ let, mail ___, ___ et. The child says the picture word, works out which part is missing, and writes that syllable in the box. The box is sized for two to four letters, and the gap may be the first or the last syllable.
G1-326.p2: A syllable cloze asks something a letter cloze does not: the child has to hear the word in parts and then spell a whole part, not one letter, from memory of its sound. The printed half is the anchor that keeps the task about syllables rather than about spelling the whole word, and the picture supplies the word without a written model. Every word on this face comes from the set whose syllable breaks are agreed by the dictionary hyphenation used across the family, so the printed boundary is never a matter of taste.
G1-326.p3: It prints on one sheet with a pencil. Use it after the write-the-word-in-syllables page, since the child now supplies the syllable rather than copying it. Two- and three-syllable words are mixed; the around-the-house draw shown here can be swapped for other themes with the same eight-card layout.

G1-328.h1: Two or Three Syllables? Split the Word and Sort It
G1-328.title: Two or Three Syllables Worksheet for 1st Grade | Free Printable PDF
G1-328.metaDescription: Two or three syllables worksheet: clap eight supermarket words in a bank, then write each with dashes between its syllables under 2 or 3. Free printable G1 PDF.
G1-328.p1: A word bank and two columns are all this 1st grade two-or-three-syllables page consists of. Across the top, inside a dashed frame, sit eight picture-and-word cards from the at-the-supermarket theme in alphabetical order — banana, blueberry, broccoli, kiwi, lemon, lettuce, tomato, toothbrush on this sheet. Below are two tall columns headed 2 syllables and 3 syllables, each with four handwriting rules. The child claps each word, decides how many parts it has, and writes it in the right column with a dash between the syllables: kiwi and lemon under 2, banana and broccoli under 3. Four words go each way.
G1-328.p2: Sorting by count is a Kindergarten task when it is done by drawing a line to a numeral; writing each word split with dashes under a heading makes it a 1st grade one, because the child has to commit to where the breaks are as well as how many. The even four-and-four split means the last word can be placed by elimination but the split itself cannot be, and a supermarket word like toothbrush — two syllables, ten letters — keeps length from being a shortcut for count.
G1-328.p3: The columns take a big first-grade hand, one word per rule. Print it as the closing page of a syllable week: the scoop page and the copy-with-dashes page come first, and this one asks for both skills at once. Other themes print into the same two-column shape.

G1-306.h1: Word Families: Read the Carpet, Then Write the Beginning
G1-306.title: Word Families Worksheet for 1st Grade | Free Printable PDF
G1-306.metaDescription: Word families worksheet: read ten -an and -at words on a carpet out loud, then write the beginning of six picture words before the printed ending. Free printable G1 PDF.
G1-306.p1: A carpet of ten words opens this 1st grade word families worksheet: two rows of five cells, each cell a word with its beginning in dark ink and its ending in coral, split by a thin line — can, fan, pan, van, swan across the top and bat, cat, hat, mat, sat beneath, on the -an and -at sheet shown here. A dashed circle at the end of each row is for a tick once the row has been read aloud. Below the carpet are six picture cards, three across and two down (a hat, a bat, a fan, a swan, a pan, a can), each with a dashed handwriting lane in which the ending is already printed in coral. The child says the picture word, finds it on the carpet, and writes its beginning on the lane in front of the ending.
G1-306.p2: The carpet is a fluency drill and the cards are a spelling check, and the order matters: every word the child will need has been read aloud, in a family, before it has to be written. Coloring the ending and printing it on the lane keeps the task on the onset — the one or two letters that change from word to word — which is where a first grader's attention belongs when the rime is the thing being learned. Alternate cells are shaded so a finger can track along the row.
G1-306.p3: It prints on a single sheet; the lanes are three-line handwriting rules, so the letters written are full size. The read-and-circle page in this family offers three printed words per picture instead of a lane, and the carpet page stretches the reading to five rows. Word families with blends move the same layout onto two-letter beginnings.

G1-330.h1: Word Families: Read the Words and Circle the One That Names the Picture
G1-330.title: Word Families Read and Circle Worksheet for 1st Grade | Free Printable PDF
G1-330.metaDescription: Word families read-and-circle worksheet: read the carpet out loud, then under each of six pictures circle the one word of three that names it. Free 1st grade PDF.
G1-330.p1: Nothing is written on this 1st grade word families read-and-circle page; the pencil only circles. The two-row carpet at the top is the same as on the read-and-write sheet — can, fan, pan, van, swan and bat, cat, hat, mat, sat on the -an and -at version shown — with a dashed circle to tick after each row is read. Below it, six cards show a picture (a bat, a pan, a cat, a fan, a hat, a van) over a stack of three word pills, the beginning of each word in dark ink and the ending in coral. Two of the three pills come from the same row of the carpet as the answer, so hat sits with sat and bat under the bat, and the child circles the one word that names the picture.
G1-330.p2: Recognition before production: this is the step before the child has to spell an onset, and it tests whether they can tell can from fan when both are in front of them. Drawing the foils from the same family is deliberate. A child who only reads the coral ending sees three words that all end the same and cannot choose; the choice has to be made on the first letter or two, which is exactly the discrimination the carpet was drilling.
G1-330.p3: It prints on one portrait sheet and takes a few minutes. Use it on the day the family is introduced, then the read-and-write page once the words are recognized. The color-the-carpet page for the same families is the fluency stretch, and word families with blends is the harder onset.

G1-331.h1: Join the Syllables and Write the Whole Word
G1-331.title: Join the Syllables Worksheet for 1st Grade | Free Printable PDF
G1-331.metaDescription: Join the syllables worksheet: two syllables are printed in order on each of six cards; read them, say them together and write the whole word. Free printable G1 PDF.
G1-331.p1: There is no carpet on this 1st grade join-the-syllables page, only six cards in two columns of three. Each card has a picture at the top, two syllable tiles joined by a plus sign under it, and a three-line handwriting rule under the tiles — trac + tor beside a tractor, read + ing, rain + coat, sweat + pants, pan + da, pep + per on the sheet shown. The tiles are printed in the right order. The child reads the first tile, then the second, says the two together as one word, and writes the whole word on the rule without the gap. Every word on this face has exactly two syllables, and the pictures are drawn from across the themes rather than from one.
G1-331.p2: The syllables are printed and the child produces the word — that is the boundary between this family and the syllable division pages, where the word is printed and the child produces the break. Reading a long word in two visible parts and then closing the gap is how first graders are shown to attack panda and tractor before they can do it silently, and writing the joined word proves that the parts were read as parts and not guessed from the picture.
G1-331.p3: Print one per child; the rule is full size and the six words are a short session. It sits between the one-syllable word-family sheets and the read-the-syllables page, where the words grow to three syllables and the picture has to be found in a bank. A single portrait page, pencil only.

G1-332.h1: Word Family Carpet: Read Five Rows, Then Color Each Picture's Word
G1-332.title: Word Family Carpet Read and Color Worksheet 1st Grade | Free Printable PDF
G1-332.metaDescription: Word family carpet worksheet: read 25 words in five rows out loud, then find each of six pictures on the carpet and color its word in that color. Free printable G1 PDF.
G1-332.p1: Five rows of five make a carpet of twenty-five words on this 1st grade word family carpet page — on the sheet shown, the -an, -at, -ock, -ug and -og families: can, fan, pan, van, swan; bat, cat, hat, mat, sat; clock, lock, rock, sock, dock; jug, mug, rug, slug, bug; dog, frog, log, fog, hog. Each cell prints the beginning in dark ink and the ending in coral, and a dashed circle ends every row for a tick once it is read. Under the carpet sit six picture cards, each with a colored dot beside the picture: a fan with pink, a bat with brown, a sock with green, a swan with purple, a slug with yellow, a frog with red. The child reads the whole carpet aloud, then finds each picture's word and colors that cell in the picture's color.
G1-332.p2: This is the fluency face of the family. The carpet is more than twice the base page's, and reading all of it before any coloring is the point — twenty-five short words across five rimes, read in order, is a minute of decoding practice with the rime held constant and the onset changing. The coloring is the check that the reading was real: the six targets come from at least three different rows, so the child has to locate a word by reading it, not by counting down one column.
G1-332.p3: It prints on one sheet and needs six colors of crayon or pencil. Use it once the read-and-write and read-and-circle pages for two families are done, as the page that mixes families. Because the carpet fans by family, a different set of rows can be printed for the next week.

G1-333.h1: Word Families with Blends: Write the Two Letters the Word Starts With
G1-333.title: Word Families with Blends Worksheet for 1st Grade | Free Printable PDF
G1-333.metaDescription: Word families with blends: read ten blend words on the carpet, then write the two-letter beginning of six picture words before the printed ending. Free G1 PDF.
G1-333.p1: Two letters go on the line instead of one on this 1st grade word families with blends page. The carpet at the top holds ten words that start with a consonant blend, the blend in dark ink and the rest in coral — flag, crab, drum, swan, blocks across the top row and clock, frog, glass, stamp, truck on the second, on the sheet shown. Six picture cards follow (a truck, a drum, a clock, a swan, a flag, a frog), each with a dashed handwriting lane in which the ending is printed in coral: uck, um, ock, an, ag, og. The child reads the carpet aloud, says each picture word, finds it, and writes the two-letter blend on the lane.
G1-333.p2: The rime is no longer the unit being learned; the blend is. Each carpet on this face is a ladder of five blends — fl, cr, dr, sw, bl on this sheet, with cl, fr, gl, st, tr and further ladders on the others — so the endings vary from word to word while the beginnings share a shape: two consonants, both heard. Printing the ending on the lane keeps the writing to those two letters, and a child who writes only one of them has shown the teacher which blend still sounds like a single letter to them.
G1-333.p3: Print it after the single-consonant word family sheets, when onsets are reliable and blends are being introduced. The layout is the base page's, so the routine is already known: carpet first, cards second. One portrait sheet with full-size handwriting lanes.

G1-334.h1: Read the Syllables, Find the Picture, Write Its Number
G1-334.title: Read the Syllables Worksheet for 1st Grade | Free Printable PDF
G1-334.metaDescription: Read the syllables worksheet: six words are printed split by hyphens; read each one and write the number of its picture from a bank of eight. Free printable G1 PDF.
G1-334.p1: Eight numbered pictures line the top of this 1st grade read-the-syllables page inside a dashed frame — a mirror, a basketball, a butterfly, a bandage, a hammer, an orange, a cookie and a dragonfly on the sheet shown. Below run six wide rows, each printing one word already split into syllables with hyphens: bas-ket-ball, ban-dage, cook-ie, but-ter-fly, or-ange, mir-ror. At the right of every row is a small dashed box. The child reads the word part by part, finds its picture in the bank, and writes the picture's number in the box. Two pictures in the bank belong to no word, so two numbers are never used.
G1-334.p2: This is decoding of longer words with the syllable breaks supplied, which is the scaffold reading programs give when a child moves from cat and fan to butterfly. The word is never shown whole; the child has to blend the parts and only then can the picture be matched, and the two distractors mean the picture cannot be found by elimination on the last row. Words run to ten letters and three syllables, with at least one three-syllable word on every sheet.
G1-334.p3: Print it as the final page of the word families sequence: the carpets and lanes before it work on single-syllable words, and this page carries the reading into multisyllable ones without asking for any writing beyond a numeral. One sheet, pencil, no coloring.

G2-315.h1: Spelling Rules: Write the Rule Letters Under Each Picture
G2-315.title: Spelling Rules Worksheet for 2nd Grade | Free Printable PDF
G2-315.metaDescription: Spelling rules worksheet: a rule box with two model words, then eight picture words with only the rule letters left blank in dashed boxes. Free printable 2nd grade PDF.
G2-315.p1: One spelling rule per sheet is the idea of this 2nd grade spelling rules worksheet, and the sheet shown is Magic e. A dashed rule box across the top prints the rule as four chips — a_e, i_e, o_e, u_e — and two model words with pictures, cake and kite, with the rule letters in coral. Eight numbered cards follow in two columns of four, each with a picture and its word spelled in spaced letters, every letter printed except the rule letters, which are dashed boxes: g _ t _ for gate, l _ m _ for lime, w _ v _ for wave, and longer words such as cheesecake, bookcase, pinecone and wardrobe with the boxes deep inside. The child reads the rule, says the picture word, and writes the missing rule letters.
G2-315.p2: The rule letters are the task and everything else is printed — that is the boundary between this page and an ordinary missing-letter sheet. A child does not have to spell wardrobe; they have to decide that the sound in robe is written o_e, and the two model words are there to be checked against. Rules in the English set include magic e, c-k-ck, ee-ea, ai-ay, the doubled ff-ll-ss-zz ending and the plural changes y to ies and f to ves, each on its own sheet with words of three to twelve letters at this level.
G2-315.p3: Print it as the first page of a rule's week. The which-one page offers two spellings to choose from, rule detective has the child find the rule inside a whole printed word, and write-the-word gives only the rule letters and asks for the rest.

G2-324.h1: Which One? Choose Between Two Spellings of the Same Sound
G2-324.title: Which One Spelling Rules Worksheet for 2nd Grade | Free Printable PDF
G2-324.metaDescription: Which one worksheet: read eight picture words with one gap each, circle the right spelling on the two chips below, then write it in. Free printable 2nd grade PDF.
G2-324.p1: A choice between two chips is what this 2nd grade which-one page asks for eight times over. The sheet shown is c or k: the rule box at the top holds only the two letters, and eight cards in two columns of four each show a small picture beside a word in spaced letters with one dashed gap — _ ey for key, _ angaroo, _ omb, _ anoe, _ ardigan, _ iwi, _ alf, and lee _ with the gap at the end. Under every word sit two chips printed c and k. The child reads the word, circles the chip that fills the gap correctly, and copies the letter into the dashed box. Four words on the sheet take c and four take k.
G2-324.p2: Offering the two candidates turns the rule into a decision the child can reason about: k before e and i, c before a, o and u, with kangaroo and canoe side by side to make the pattern visible. That is a different skill from the base page, where nothing is offered and the rule letters come from memory, and it is the right first step for a spelling that has two legitimate forms. The English set runs this face over the pair rules — c or k, ee or ea, ai or ay — one pair per sheet.
G2-324.p3: It prints on one page and most children finish it quickly, since each card is one circle and one letter. Use it before the sort-by-rule page, which uses the same pair but asks for the whole word to be written into a bin. Words run up to ten letters and none are labeled with their answer.

G2-325.h1: Rule Detective: Find the Rule Letters Inside the Whole Word
G2-325.title: Rule Detective Spelling Worksheet for 2nd Grade | Free Printable PDF
G2-325.metaDescription: Rule detective worksheet: eight words are printed in full; read each, circle the rule letters inside it, then copy them into the small box. Free printable 2nd grade PDF.
G2-325.p1: Every word is printed in full on this 2nd grade rule detective page, and the child's job is to find the rule inside it. The sheet shown is Magic e, with the same rule box as the base page — the four chips a_e, i_e, o_e, u_e and the models cake and kite — over eight cards in two columns: a scale, a cube, an airplane, a lime, a vase, a rake, a porcupine and a nose, each word spelled out in spaced letters with a small dashed box after it. The child reads the word, circles the rule letters where they sit — the a and the final e of scale, the i and e at the end of porcupine — and copies just those letters into the box.
G2-325.p2: Reading a rule is not the same as writing one, and this face works on the reading side: a child who can spot that porcupine ends in an i_e pattern is ready to read new words with it, whether or not they can yet spell them. No foil words are mixed in on this face, so every word on the sheet obeys the rule and the hunt is always for where, not whether. Words run to nine letters, and the longer ones are chosen so that the rule letters are not simply the last two.
G2-325.p3: Print it in the same week as the base spelling rules page for the same rule; the base writes the letters, this one finds them, and the two together cover the rule from both sides. A pencil circle and two or three copied letters per card make it a short sheet. Write-the-word is the harder face, where those same rule letters are the only thing printed.

G2-326.h1: Sort by Spelling Rule: Write Each Picture Word in Its Bin
G2-326.title: Sort by Spelling Rule Worksheet for 2nd Grade | Free Printable PDF
G2-326.metaDescription: Sort by spelling rule worksheet: say eight picture words, decide which of two spellings each uses, and write it in that bin, one per line. Free printable 2nd grade PDF.
G2-326.p1: Eight unlabeled pictures and two bins are the whole of this 2nd grade sort-by-spelling-rule page. The sheet shown is c or k: the rule box prints the two letters, a dashed strip beneath it holds the picture bank — a desk, a cardigan, a baker, a donkey, a car, a turkey, a cardinal and a key — and below are two tall bins headed with a c chip and a k chip, five handwriting rules in each. The child says each picture word, decides which letter spells its hard-c sound, and writes the whole word into that bin, one per line. Three words go to one bin and five to the other on this sheet, so the two columns do not fill evenly.
G2-326.p2: No word is written for the child here, which makes it the most demanding of the family's c-or-k faces: the picture has to be named, the rule applied to the sound, and the whole word spelled into the bin. The uneven three-and-five split is deliberate — a child cannot finish one bin and put the rest in the other — and words like desk and turkey put the k at the end rather than the front, so the sort is by spelling, not by first letter. The pair rules ee-ea and ai-ay print in the same two-bin shape.
G2-326.p3: The bins take a large hand and the page prints on one sheet. Use it after the which-one page has made the pair familiar and before a dictation. A teacher checking the sheet reads down each bin once; a word in the wrong bin and a word misspelled in the right bin are two different errors.

G2-327.h1: Write the Word: Only the Rule Letters Are Given
G2-327.title: Write the Whole Word Spelling Worksheet for 2nd Grade | Free Printable PDF
G2-327.metaDescription: Write the word worksheet: the rule letters are printed in orange under each of eight pictures; say the word and write every other letter. Free printable 2nd grade PDF.
G2-327.p1: The base page turned inside out: on this 2nd grade write-the-word sheet only the rule letters are printed, in orange, and every other letter is an empty box. The Magic e version shown keeps the rule box with its four chips and the models cake and kite, then gives eight cards in two columns — a wave, a gate, a whale, a rake, a pancake, a pinecone, a lime and a roll of tape — each with a row of dashed boxes in which the vowel and the final e stand printed: _ a _ e for gate, _ _ a _ e for whale, _ _ _ _ a _ e for pancake. The child says the picture word and writes all the other letters into the boxes.
G2-327.p2: Anchoring the rule letters and asking for the rest reverses the demand of the base page, and the reversal matters for a rule like magic e: the child is shown that the a and the e belong together and has to build the consonants around them, which is how the split pattern is held in mind when reading. The number of boxes tells the child how long the word is, so pancake and pinecone are not guesses. Words run to eight letters on this face, a little shorter than the base so the boxes stay large.
G2-327.p3: Print it at the end of a rule's week, after the base and rule detective pages, as the page where the child writes the most. A rule that has no letter pair, such as magic e, uses this face and the detective face; the pair rules add which-one and sort. One sheet in portrait with a pencil.

G2-328.h1: Plurals That Change the Spelling: y to ies, f to ves
G2-328.title: Plural Spelling Rules Worksheet y to ies, f to ves | Free Printable PDF
G2-328.metaDescription: Plural spelling worksheet: read the word for one beside its picture, then write the changed ending for many: candy to candies, wolf to wolves. Free printable G2 PDF.
G2-328.p1: Six rows, each with a singular on the left and a plural to finish on the right, make up this 2nd grade plural spelling page. The rule box at the top prints two chips, ies and ves, and two worked models with pictures: cherry to cherries and leaf to leaves, the changed ending in coral. Each row below shows one picture with its word in spaced letters — candy, scarf, calf, bunny, elf, wolf on the sheet shown — and then three small copies of the picture beside the word's stem with a dashed box where the ending goes: cand ___, scar ___, cal ___. The child reads the word for one and writes the ending that makes it the word for many.
G2-328.p2: This is the one face of the family where the plural is the task rather than a vowel or consonant pattern, and it covers the two changes that trip second graders: y after a consonant becomes ies, and a final f or fe becomes ves. Printing the stem and boxing only the ending keeps the writing to the part that changes, so a child who writes candys or wolfs has made the exact error the rule exists to fix. The three little pictures make the word for many visible without a number being written.
G2-328.p3: Print it after regular plurals are secure; the Kindergarten and 1st grade singular-and-plural pages handle the ones that just add s. The English version pairs the y and f rules on one sheet, with six words of up to eight letters. One page in portrait with a pencil, and the rule box doubles as the answer key for a parent.

G1-307.title: Opposites Worksheet for 1st Grade | Free Printable PDF
G1-307.metaDescription: Opposites worksheet: read the word on each of eight cards, find its opposite in the word bank and write it on the line. Free printable 1st grade PDF.
G1-307.p1: This 1st grade opposites worksheet prints a dashed word bank of eight words across the top — wet, strong, short, heavy, big, night, quiet, cold — and eight numbered cards below it, two across and four down. Each card carries one word in large type beside a double-headed arrow: day, dry, light, loud, hot, weak, small, tall. Under the word sits a three-line handwriting rule. The child reads the card, hunts through the bank for the word that means the opposite, and writes it on the rule. Every bank word is used exactly once, so a card the child cannot solve at first can be reached by elimination at the end.
G1-307.p2: The child works with the word that means the opposite, not with a picture of something big or small, and that is what makes this a vocabulary page rather than a comparison page. Pairs such as day and night or hot and cold are already in a first grader's speech; pairs such as heavy and light or strong and weak ask for a little more thought, and light appears here as the opposite of heavy, not of dark, which is a distinction worth saying aloud. The teacher listens for the child reading the card word before searching the bank; a child who starts from the bank and guesses is matching shapes, not meanings.
G1-307.p3: It prints on a single sheet with room for a name and date. The opposites-with-pictures page is the Kindergarten step before this one, and the opposites-in-a-sentence page carries the same pairs into full sentences.

K-351.h1: Opposites with Pictures: Match the Opposites
K-351.title: Opposites with Pictures Worksheet for Kindergarten | Free Printable PDF
K-351.metaDescription: Opposites with pictures: six picture-and-word cards on the left, six on the right; draw a line from each picture to its opposite. Free printable Kindergarten PDF.
K-351.p1: Twelve picture cards fill this Kindergarten opposites page, six down the left and six down the right, each with a large color picture and its word printed beside it. On the left: a pillow for soft, a puppy for big, an elephant for heavy, a campfire for hot, a sun for day, a candy for sweet. On the right, shuffled: a snowflake for cold, a rock for hard, a lemon for sour, a smaller puppy for small, a feather for light, a moon for night. A dot sits at the inner edge of every card, and the child draws a line from dot to dot to join each picture to the one that shows its opposite. Nothing is written.
K-351.p2: Because both members of every pair are pictured and labeled, a child who cannot yet read the words can still solve the page from the pictures and then look at the word that came with the answer — which is exactly how opposite pairs enter a kindergartner's vocabulary. The pairs mix physical qualities the child can feel (soft and hard, hot and cold, heavy and light) with taste and time (sweet and sour, day and night). Only one pair, big and small, is shown by the same animal drawn at two sizes; every other pair is two different things. The teacher asks the child to say both words as the line is drawn: soft, hard.
K-351.p3: The page is a matching page, so it prints cleanly on one sheet and needs only a pencil or crayon. It is the picture-first entry to this family; the 1st grade write-the-opposite page asks the child to write the partner word from a bank instead of drawing to it, and the opposite-or-the-same page adds a synonym decoy to each row for children who already know the pairs.

G1-335.h1: Opposites in a Sentence: Finish It with the Opposite Word
G1-335.title: Opposites in a Sentence Worksheet for 1st Grade | Free Printable PDF
G1-335.metaDescription: Opposites in a sentence: read The snail is not fast, then write the opposite word, slow, on the line under it. Six sentences, a bank of six words. Free 1st grade PDF.
G1-335.p1: Each of the six rows on this 1st grade opposites-in-a-sentence page begins with a short sentence built around not: The snail is not fast. The feather is not heavy. Max is not sad today. The lemon is not sweet. The snowflake is not hot. The moon is out, it is not day. A picture of the snail, feather, face, lemon, snowflake or moon sits at the left of the row, and under the sentence a second line waits to be finished: It is ______. The child writes the opposite of the word after not — slow, light, happy, sour, cold, night — choosing from a six-word bank in a dashed box at the top. Six sentences, six bank words, no word used twice.
G1-335.p2: The not-frame turns an isolated word pair into a piece of grammar the child already uses: if something is not fast, it is slow. That is a different skill from matching words on cards, because the child has to locate the key word inside a sentence, hold its meaning, and produce the partner in a new sentence. The picture beside each row confirms the answer without giving the word away — the snail looks slow, the lemon looks sour. The teacher is listening for the child to read the whole first sentence aloud before writing; the word after not is the only word that matters, and finding it is the reading work.
G1-335.p3: Print one per child; the handwriting rule in each row is a full three-line guide, so this doubles as a sentence-copying page. The base write-the-opposite page practices the same pairs on bare cards without a sentence, and the pair-up page removes the bank so the child finds both words of each pair alone. Use this page after the cards and before the pair-up.

G1-336.h1: Pair Up the Opposites: Find Both Words Yourself
G1-336.title: Pair Up the Opposites Worksheet for 1st Grade | Free Printable PDF
G1-336.metaDescription: Pair up the opposites: twelve loose words at the top and no pairs given. Find each pair and write it on a line, one word each side of the arrow. Free 1st grade PDF.
G1-336.p1: Nothing on this 1st grade opposites page tells the child which word goes with which. Twelve loose words sit in a bank across the top — dark, low, sweet, bright, slow, dry, high, hard, wet, sour, soft, fast — and below them are six numbered rows, each with two handwriting rules and a double-headed arrow between them. The child reads through the bank, spots two words that are opposites, and writes the pair on a row, one word on each side of the arrow: dark on the left, bright on the right. Six rows, six pairs, and every word in the bank used exactly once.
G1-336.p2: This is the hardest of the word-only opposites pages, because no card gives the child a starting word. Both halves of every pair must be found by scanning and comparing, which is the real test of whether the pairs are known rather than recognized. The bank deliberately includes near-neighbors: hard could tempt a child toward soft or toward easy, but easy is not there; wet and dry, high and low, fast and slow have to be sorted out of one shuffled set. The teacher watches a child who writes the first six words down the left side and then hunts for partners — that is a fine strategy, and the arrow reminds the child that either order is correct.
G1-336.p3: The page needs nothing but a pencil; the writing rules are full-size so both words fit. If it proves too open, step back to the opposites-in-a-sentence page, where a not-sentence supplies the first word of each pair, or to the base page, where each card prints one word and the bank holds the other. The opposite-or-the-same page is the natural follow-up: it keeps the child choosing between words but adds a synonym to reject.

G1-337.h1: Opposite or the Same? Circle the Opposite, Not the Synonym
G1-337.title: Opposite or the Same Worksheet for 1st Grade | Free Printable PDF
G1-337.metaDescription: Opposite or the same: six words, three choices under each — one opposite, one synonym, one stray word. Circle only the opposite. Free printable 1st grade PDF.
G1-337.p1: Six word rows fill this 1st grade opposites page, and each is a small trap. The row's word — rough, big, strong, fast, loud, happy — is printed in large type beside an arrow, and three words in outlined chips sit under it. One chip means the opposite (smooth), one means the same (bumpy), and one is an unrelated word from another pair (night). The child circles the opposite and leaves the synonym alone. All six rows follow that pattern: big with small, large and wet; strong with weak, tough and day; fast with slow, quick and soft; loud with quiet, noisy and new; happy with sad, glad and cold.
G1-337.p2: Putting a synonym next to the antonym is what makes this page teach something the card pages cannot. A child who has learned that the answer is the word that goes with rough will circle bumpy, because bumpy also goes with rough; only a child who is thinking about the direction of meaning — the other end of the scale — chooses smooth. That is the distinction 1st grade vocabulary work is trying to build, and the stray third word keeps the choice from collapsing into a coin toss between two related words. The teacher asks a child who circled the synonym to say both chip words in a sentence about the same object; the error usually corrects itself out loud.
G1-337.p3: No writing is required, so the page works as a quick check at the end of an opposites unit or as a warm-up before the pair-up page. Keep the base write-the-opposite page and the opposites-in-a-sentence page for the children who still need to produce the word; this one is for children who can already produce it and need to sharpen the meaning. The 2nd grade antonyms-with-a-prefix page moves on to opposites built with un-, dis- and in-.

G2-320.h1: Antonyms with un-, dis- and in-: Build the Opposite Word
G2-320.title: Antonyms with un-, dis-, in- Worksheet for 2nd Grade | Free Printable PDF
G2-320.metaDescription: Antonyms with prefixes: eight base words — kind, lucky, obey, visible, safe, tidy — pick un-, dis- or in- and write the new opposite word. Free 2nd grade PDF.
G2-320.p1: This 2nd grade antonyms page, the last page in the opposites family, opens with three prefix chips in a row — un-, dis-, in- — and then lists eight numbered base words down the left: kind, lucky, obey, happy, visible, safe, tidy, fair. Beside each word is an arrow and a handwriting rule. The child picks the prefix that turns the word into its opposite and writes the whole new word on the rule: unkind, unlucky, disobey, unhappy, invisible, unsafe, untidy, unfair. The prefixes are not assigned per row, so the child has to try each one in the head and hear which makes a real word. Most take un-; obey wants dis- and visible wants in-.
G2-320.p2: The opposites of 1st grade were separate words — hot and cold, big and small. This page shows the other way English makes an antonym: by putting a negative prefix on the front of a word the child already knows. That is the morphology 2nd graders are asked to use when they meet an unfamiliar word, and it works best when the child hears that the prefix means not: unkind is not kind, invisible is not visible. The teacher watches for two errors — a child who writes the prefix alone on the line instead of the whole word, and a child who attaches un- to every word because it fits most of them; disobey and invisible are the rows that reveal the second.
G2-320.p3: It prints as one clean sheet with a name line and can be corrected against the prefix chips at the top. The page belongs after the 1st grade opposites family — the base cards, the sentence page and the opposite-or-the-same page — because it assumes the child already knows what an antonym is and now needs the spelling rule. Pair it with a spelling-rules page on prefixes if the class is collecting word parts.

G1-308.h1: Read and Do: Follow the Instructions
G1-308.title: Read and Do Worksheet for 1st Grade – Animals | Free Printable PDF
G1-308.metaDescription: Read and do worksheet: a row of eight animal pictures and six sentences — circle the first picture, cross out the swan, write how many seagulls. Free 1st grade PDF.
G1-308.p1: A strip of eight animal pictures runs across the top of this 1st grade read-and-do worksheet, with a small flag at the left end and an arrow showing the direction to count: a donkey, a seagull, a swan, a whale, another seagull, a fox, a leopard, a second whale. Under the strip are six numbered sentences, each with a little dashed box at the right. Circle the first picture. Underline the second seagull. Put a check mark under the last picture. Cross out the swan. Write how many seagulls there are. Underline the leopard. The child reads a sentence, does exactly that to the picture row with a pencil, and checks the box to show the row is done.
G1-308.p2: Every sentence uses a different pencil action, and that is the point: circle, underline, cross out, check mark and write each demand that the child read to the end of the sentence and not act on the first noun. Some sentences name an animal (the swan), some name a place in the row (the first picture, the last picture), and one asks for a count written in a box, so the same short strip is read five or six different ways. The teacher is watching for a child who circles the first animal named in every row — that child is decoding words, not yet reading instructions — and for the check box being ticked before the action is done.
G1-308.p3: The page prints in color on one sheet and is finished in a few minutes, which makes it a good independent-reading task while a group works with the teacher. The read-and-circle page keeps one action only, the two-step page puts two actions in each sentence, and the true-or-false page turns the instructions into statements to judge.

G1-338.h1: Read and Circle: Find the Zoo Animal the Sentence Names
G1-338.title: Read and Circle Worksheet for 1st Grade – Zoo Animals | Free Printable PDF
G1-338.metaDescription: Read and circle: one row of zoo animals, six sentences that each name one animal or all of a kind — circle the giraffe, circle all the antelopes. Free 1st grade PDF.
G1-338.p1: One pencil action only on this 1st grade read-and-do page, the read-and-circle face: draw a circle. A row of eight zoo animals sits at the top — an antelope, a cheetah, an elephant, a second antelope, a giraffe, a fox, a panda and a third antelope — and the six sentences below it all begin the same way: Circle the giraffe. Circle all the antelopes. Circle the panda. Circle the cheetah. Circle the fox. Circle the elephant. Each sentence ends in a little dashed box the child checks when the circle is drawn. Because the verb never changes, the whole reading load falls on the noun, and on the difference between the giraffe and all the antelopes.
G1-338.p2: This is the gentlest face in the read-and-do family, meant for a child who is just moving from reading words to reading for a purpose. The noun is the only thing to find, and it is found in a picture the child can already name, so the page rewards matching the printed word to the spoken animal name. The single sentence with all in it is the one that matters: a child who circles one antelope has read the noun but not the sentence, and the teacher points to the word all and asks how many there are. Zoo animals keep the nouns long and distinct — cheetah, elephant, panda — so sound-it-out reading has real work to do.
G1-338.p3: Print it as a first independent reading task and expect it to take five minutes. When the child circles reliably, move to the base read-and-do page, which mixes circle with underline, cross out, check mark and write, and then to the two-step page. The true-or-false page uses the same kind of picture strip but asks the child to judge a statement instead of act on it.

G1-339.h1: Read and Do: Two-Step Instructions in One Sentence
G1-339.title: Two-Step Instructions Worksheet for 1st Grade | Free Printable PDF
G1-339.metaDescription: Two-step instructions: each of four sentences asks for two pencil actions on a row of farm animals — underline all the cows and check the llama. Free 1st grade PDF.
G1-339.p1: Four long sentences instead of six short ones make up this 1st grade two-step read-and-do page. The picture row at the top holds eight farm animals — a bee, a cow, a chick, a second cow, two more bees, a lamb and a llama — and each sentence joins two pencil actions with and: Write how many cows there are and cross out the third bee. Underline all the cows and put a check mark under the llama. Underline the lamb and cross out the chick. Circle the second bee and put a check mark under the first picture. The first row also carries a small box for the number. The child reads to the period before touching the pencil, then does both halves and checks the box.
G1-339.p2: Two actions in one sentence is the step where reading becomes following directions. A child who begins after the first clause will underline the cows and stop, and the second half is never done; the instruction on the page says it plainly — read it to the end before you start. The sentences also mix the ways a picture can be named: by animal (the lamb), by count (the third bee, the second bee), by all (all the cows) and by place (the first picture). The teacher looks at the check box last: it should be ticked only when both marks are on the strip, and asking the child to point to the two things done is the fastest check.
G1-339.p3: The page prints on one sheet with generous row height, so there is room for a child to reread. Use it after the base read-and-do page, where every sentence has one action, and before the first-second-between page, which makes the position words the whole task. Children who rush can go back to the read-and-circle page for a few days, where the verb never changes and only the noun has to be found.

G1-340.h1: Read and Do: First, Second, Between — Find the Picture by Its Place
G1-340.title: Read and Do: First, Second, Between for 1st Grade | Free Printable PDF
G1-340.metaDescription: First, second, between: count along a row of fruits from the flag and find each picture by its place — the second fig, the one right of the avocado. Free 1st grade PDF.
G1-340.p1: Position words carry every sentence on this 1st grade read-and-do page. The row of eight fruits at the top — a pineapple, a blackberry, an avocado, a fig, a second blackberry, a second fig, two persimmons — starts at a small flag, and the child counts from the flag to find each picture by its place before doing anything to it. Cross out the last picture. Cross out the second blackberry. Circle the picture between the pineapple and the avocado. Put a check mark under the second fig. Circle the picture to the right of the avocado. Underline the first picture. Six sentences, six dashed boxes to check, four different pencil actions.
G1-340.p2: The ordinal is read inside a full sentence here, which is what separates this page from a worksheet that simply labels 1st, 2nd, 3rd. The second blackberry is not the second picture; it is the second of the blackberries, and a child has to count only the blackberries to find it. Between and to the right of ask for the same kind of thinking with two anchors instead of one. The flag settles the direction so that left and right mean the same thing for every child. The teacher listens for the counting — first, second — and watches for the child who circles the first fig when the sentence said the second.
G1-340.p3: A single printed sheet, done with a pencil, and quick to check because every answer is a mark on the strip. It sits after the base read-and-do page in this family, which uses first and last but not between or to the right of, and pairs naturally with an ordinal numbers page if the class is learning the words themselves. The two-step page combines a position cue with a second action in one sentence.

G1-341.h1: Read and Check: True or False About the Picture Row
G1-341.title: True or False Reading Worksheet for 1st Grade – Toys | Free Printable PDF
G1-341.metaDescription: True or false: a row of eight toys and six statements about it — the third picture is the bicycle, there are three trucks. Circle true or false. Free 1st grade PDF.
G1-341.p1: Nothing is circled in the picture row on this 1st grade read-and-do page, the true-or-false face; the row is only looked at. Eight toys sit across the top — a bicycle, a boat, a second bicycle, a sandbox, a truck, a robot, a second truck and a doll — and under them six statements each end in two chips, true and false. The third picture is the bicycle. There are four sandboxes in the row. The row starts with the bicycle. There are three trucks in the row. There are more than three boats in the row. The last picture is the doll. The child reads the statement, checks it against the row, and circles the chip that fits. Three of the six are true and three are false.
G1-341.p2: Judging a sentence is a different act from obeying one. In the other read-and-do pages the child does what the words say; here the words make a claim and the pictures decide whether it is right, which is the first step toward reading comprehension questions. The statements probe count (three trucks — there are two), position (the third picture, the last picture, starts with) and comparison (more than three boats), so a child cannot answer from the nouns alone. The teacher asks a child who marked false to say what would make it true — two trucks, not three — which shows whether the row was actually counted.
G1-341.p3: It prints on one sheet with large true and false chips that a first grader can circle without crowding. Keep this page for the end of the read-and-do sequence: the base page, the read-and-circle page and the two-step page all have the child marking the strip, and this one turns the same strip into evidence. It pairs with a short reading-comprehension page as the next step.

G1-342.h1: Read and Draw: Draw Exactly What the Sentence Says
G1-342.title: Read and Draw Worksheet for 1st Grade – Vehicles | Free Printable PDF
G1-342.metaDescription: Read and draw: six boxes, six sentences about vehicles — draw three small ships, draw four cars in a row, draw four big subways. No pictures to copy. Free 1st grade PDF.
G1-342.p1: There is no picture row on this 1st grade read-and-do page, the read-and-draw face, and that is the whole idea. Six large cards, two across and three down, each print one sentence about vehicles above an empty dashed box: Draw three small ships in the box. Draw three small bicycles in the box. Draw two small ambulances in the box. Draw four cars in a row. Draw four subways. Make them big. Draw four cranes in the box. The child reads the sentence and draws exactly what it says — the right vehicle, the right number, small or big, in a row when it says so. Every box is the same size, so the size words have to come from the reading.
G1-342.p2: Drawing from text is comprehension you can see. When a sentence says three small ships and the box shows two large ones, the teacher knows which word was skipped without asking a question. The numbers stay between two and four so counting never becomes the obstacle, and most of the vehicles are ones a first grader can sketch in outline — a car, a bicycle, a ship. The page does not ask for good drawings; it asks for the right number of the right thing, and a row of four boxes labeled car is a full answer. The teacher reads the sentence back with the child while looking at the box: three? small? ships?
G1-342.p3: Print it in black and white if you like — nothing on the page is in color and the boxes are for pencil. It is the one face of the read-and-do family with no pictures to point at, so use it last, after the base page and the true-or-false page, when the child can already act on a sentence and now has to imagine it. A write-rows or reading-comprehension page carries on from here.

G1-309.title: Rhyming Words Worksheet for 1st Grade | Free Printable PDF
G1-309.metaDescription: Rhyming words worksheet: say the first picture, circle the one of three that rhymes with it and write its word — boat and coat, hat and bat. Six rows. Free 1st grade PDF.
G1-309.p1: Six rows, each a small rhyming puzzle, make up this 1st grade rhyming-words worksheet. At the left of every row is one boxed picture — a boat, a bee, a hat, a bun, a dog, a jar — followed by a sound mark and three pictures in dotted circles. Only one of the three rhymes: the boat's row offers a house, a flag and a coat; the hat's row a rose, a bat and a vest; the dog's row a frog, a snail and a skirt. The child says the first picture out loud, says the three choices, circles the one that rhymes, and writes that word on the handwriting rule at the right of the row. The child hears the rhyme and writes the rhyming word; nothing is joined by a line.
G1-309.p2: Rhyme is the first sound skill most children master, and this page moves it from the ear to the pencil. The two wrong choices in each row are drawn from other rhyme families, so a child who says the words will hear the mismatch at once, and the right answer is always a word whose rhyme is spelled the same way — bat for hat, coat for boat, car for jar — which means the child can spell the answer by copying the ending sound. The teacher listens for the saying: a child who circles silently is matching pictures, and the page has no way to reward that. Write the anchor word above the row if the child needs the spelling in view.
G1-309.p3: It prints on one sheet with a full three-line rule per row. The rhyme-or-not page is the Kindergarten judgment step before this, and the sort-the-rhymes and rhyme-strings pages send the child to a bank of words instead of three pictures.

K-352.h1: Rhyme or Not? Tick If They Rhyme, Cross If They Don't
K-352.title: Rhyme or Not Worksheet for Kindergarten | Free Printable PDF
K-352.metaDescription: Rhyme or not: eight pairs of pictures — say both words, circle the tick if they rhyme (log and frog) or the cross if they do not (nail and cake). Free Kindergarten PDF.
K-352.p1: Eight picture pairs are laid out two across and four down on this Kindergarten rhyming-words page, and under each pair sit two circles, one with a tick and one with a cross. A guitar and a jar. A bun and a sun. A nail and a cake. A hand and a can. A log and a frog. A bat and a hat. A map and a truck. A sled and a boat. The child says both pictures out loud, decides whether the two words rhyme, and circles the tick or the cross. Four pairs rhyme and four do not. There is nothing to write and nothing to draw between the cards.
K-352.p2: Recognizing a rhyme comes before producing one, and this page asks only for the recognition. The non-rhyming pairs are built so that they do not rhyme by any stretch — nail and cake share a long a but nothing after it, hand and can start alike and end differently — so a child who says the words slowly can hear the answer without help. A guitar and a jar rhyme on the stressed syllable, which is a good moment to show that rhyme lives at the end of a word. The teacher listens for both words being said; a child who circles the cross for map and truck without speaking may be right by luck.
K-352.p3: The page prints on one sheet and can be done with a crayon. It is the entry point of the family: the 1st grade rhyme-and-write page asks the child to pick the rhyme from three pictures and write it, and the sort-the-rhymes page has the child write several words under a picture head. Use this one with children who are still learning what the word rhyme means.

G1-343.h1: Sort the Rhymes: Write Each Bank Word Under Its Rhyme Head
G1-343.title: Sort the Rhymes Worksheet for 1st Grade | Free Printable PDF
G1-343.metaDescription: Sort the rhymes: six numbered pictures in a bank, three big head pictures below — dog, star, cat. Write each bank word under its rhyming picture. Free 1st grade PDF.
G1-343.p1: A numbered picture bank runs across the top of this 1st grade rhyming-words page — a log, a car, a frog, a bat, a guitar, a hat — and beneath it three tall columns, each headed by one big picture: a dog, a star, a cat. Two handwriting rules wait in every column. The child says each bank picture, finds the head picture it rhymes with, and writes its word on a line in that column: log and frog under the dog, car and guitar under the star, bat and hat under the cat. Six bank words, three columns, two words each, and the head words themselves are never written.
G1-343.p2: Sorting is where a rhyme becomes a family. The rhyme-and-write page asks the child to find one partner for one picture; here three rhyme heads are open at once and every bank word has to be tested against all three before it is placed. That is harder than it looks for a six-year-old, because the bank is spoken, not read — the words are pictures, and the child supplies the spelling from the sound. The teacher can see the whole result at a glance: a column with three words or one word tells you which rhyme the child could not hear. Guitar under the star is the row worth talking about.
G1-343.p3: It prints on one sheet with columns wide enough for a first grader's handwriting. Use it after the rhyme-and-write page and before the rhyme-strings page, where the bank is words rather than pictures and some words fit nowhere. The finish-the-rhyme page changes the format completely, giving the child two lines of verse and one blank to fill.

G1-344.h1: Finish the Rhyme: Write the Missing Word in Six Short Verses
G1-344.title: Finish the Rhyme Worksheet for 1st Grade | Free Printable PDF
G1-344.metaDescription: Finish the rhyme: six two-line verses, each ending in a blank — We had some fun in the sun, and ate a sticky ___. A picture shows the missing word. Free 1st grade PDF.
G1-344.p1: Two lines of verse and one blank: that is each of the six cards on this 1st grade rhyming-words page.
