The first line ends in the rhyme word and the second line stops at a blank: We had some fun in the sun, and ate a sticky ______. At night I sleep in my warm bed, by day I ride my snowy ______. Up in the sky I saw a star, and down the road I saw a ______. A picture at the left of each card — a bun, a sled, a car, a frog, a spoon, a flag — shows the missing word, so the child reads the two lines out loud, hears that the last word must rhyme with sun or bed or star, and writes it on the handwriting rule. The cow jumps over the moon in the fifth verse, and the dish runs off with the spoon.
G1-344.p2: This is the face of the family that connects rhyme to reading. The other pages work with single words; here the rhyme sits at the end of a line the child has to read, with rhythm and sense pulling toward the answer at the same time as the sound does. A child who cannot yet decode every word can still finish the verse from the picture and the rhyme, which is exactly how nursery rhymes teach reading in the first place. The teacher reads the first line with the child and stops at the blank; the pause is where the rhyme is heard. Every answer is a short word whose rhyme is spelled like its partner.
G1-344.p3: The verses are printed in a large reading size and the page prints on one sheet. It works well read aloud in a group before anyone writes. The rhyme-and-write page and the sort-the-rhymes page are the picture-only steps before it, and the write-your-own-rhymes page is the one after, where no verse and no bank are given and the child invents the rhyming words.

G1-345.h1: Rhyme Strings: Two Rhymes for Each Picture, and Words That Fit Nowhere
G1-345.title: Rhyme Strings Worksheet for 1st Grade | Free Printable PDF
G1-345.metaDescription: Rhyme strings: four pictures — key, frog, hat, star — and a bank of twelve words. Write the two that rhyme with each picture; four fit nowhere. Free 1st grade PDF.
G1-345.p1: Twelve words sit in a dashed bank at the top of this 1st grade rhyming-words page — dog, cat, pie, tree, goat, bat, plum, jar, bed, car, bee, log — and below them four large picture cards, each with two empty handwriting rules beside it: a key, a frog, a hat, a star. The child says the picture, reads through the bank for the two words that rhyme with it, and writes them on its lines: tree and bee for the key, dog and log for the frog, cat and bat for the hat, jar and car for the star. Four bank words — pie, goat, plum, bed — rhyme with nothing on the page and are left where they are.
G1-345.p2: This is the one rhyming page where the child reads the bank and rejects words. Eight of the twelve have a home and four are foils from other rhyme families, so finishing the page means deciding, for every word, whether it belongs anywhere — a small act of judgment the picture-bank pages do not ask for. Two rhymes per picture also builds the idea of a rhyme string: not a pair but a set, dog, frog, log, that could go on. The teacher looks at the leftovers: if bed or plum has been written under a picture, the child is matching by vowel or by first letter rather than by the end of the word.
G1-345.p3: It prints on one sheet with two full rules per card. Use it after the sort-the-rhymes page, which has the same shape but a picture bank and no foils. The write-your-own-rhymes page removes the bank entirely; the finish-the-rhyme page puts the missing rhyme at the end of a line of verse instead.

G1-346.h1: Write Your Own Rhymes: Two Words That Rhyme with Each Printed Word
G1-346.title: Write Your Own Rhymes Worksheet for 1st Grade | Free Printable PDF
G1-346.metaDescription: Write your own rhymes: six picture cards with the word printed — tree, guitar, coat, bat, log, bun. Think of two rhyming words, one per line. Free 1st grade PDF.
G1-346.p1: Nothing is supplied on this 1st grade rhyming-words page except a word and its picture. Six cards, two across and three down, each show a picture with its word printed in large type beside it: tree, guitar, coat, bat, log, bun. Under each word are two handwriting rules and nothing else — no bank, no choices, no pictures to circle. The child reads the word, thinks of two words that rhyme with it, and writes one on each line. There is no single right answer: bee and key, sea and three, or any two real words that rhyme with tree all count.
G1-346.p2: Producing a rhyme is the last step of the skill, and it is the one that shows whether the child owns it. On every other page in this family the rhyming word is somewhere on the paper; here it has to come out of the child's own vocabulary and be spelled from sound, which makes the page part rhyme and part invented spelling. That is fine — cote for coat is a correct rhyme with a spelling to fix later, and the teacher should read the answers aloud rather than check them against a list. Guitar is the stretch card; car and star are the easy rhymes, and a child who finds jar has been listening to the end of the word.
G1-346.p3: The page prints on one sheet and the printed word is large enough for a child to copy the ending. The answer key lists the common rhymes for each word as examples, not as the only accepted answers. Keep this page for the end of the rhyming-words sequence, after the rhyme-and-write page and the rhyme-strings page; a child who struggles here should go back to the bank pages, where the words are supplied.

G2-316.title: Compound Words Worksheet for 2nd Grade | Free Printable PDF
G2-316.metaDescription: Compound words worksheet: name the two pictures, join the words and write the new one — star + fish = starfish, rain + coat = raincoat. Eight rows. Free 2nd grade PDF.
G2-316.p1: Eight rows run down this 2nd grade compound-words worksheet, and every row is a little equation: a picture, a plus sign, a second picture, an equals sign, and a handwriting rule. A water bottle plus a melon. A bird plus a house. A wedge of cheese plus a slice of cake. A basket plus a ball. A star plus a fish. An arm plus a chair. A rain cloud plus a coat. A sun plus a flower. The child names the two pictures, says the two words together, and writes the new word on the rule: watermelon, birdhouse, cheesecake, basketball, starfish, armchair, raincoat, sunflower. Nothing is printed except the pictures, so the spelling of both halves comes from the child.
G2-316.p2: Two words make a new word with a new meaning — that is the whole lesson, and the pictures make it visible in a way a word list cannot. A starfish is not a star and not a fish; a birdhouse is a house for a bird, not a bird that is a house. Saying the two names and then running them together lets the child hear the compound as one word with one stress, and writing it without a space is the spelling habit 2nd grade is after. The teacher watches for a child who writes the two words with a gap between them and asks whether it is one thing or two; the picture answers the question.
G2-316.p3: It prints on one sheet with eight full rules. The split-the-compound page runs the same idea backward — the whole word is printed and the child marks where it breaks — and the compound-detective page mixes real compounds with words that only look like two words.

G2-330.h1: Split the Compound: Draw a Line Where the Second Word Starts
G2-330.title: Split the Compound Word Worksheet for 2nd Grade | Free Printable PDF
G2-330.metaDescription: Split the compound: each whole word is printed letter by letter beside its picture — sandcastle, scarecrow. Draw a line where the second word begins. Free 2nd grade PDF.
G2-330.p1: The whole word is already on the page in this 2nd grade compound-words face: eight compounds, one to a row, each spelled out in spaced letters along a baseline with its picture at the left. B l u e b e l l beside a blue flower, b o o k s h e l f beside a shelf of books, then sandcastle, scarecrow, rainbow, buttercup, keyboard and earthworm. The child reads the whole word, finds the place where the first word ends and the second begins, and draws one vertical line through that gap: blue | bell, book | shelf, sand | castle. One line per word, nothing to write.
G2-330.p2: Cutting a compound is the reverse of building one, and it is the skill that pays off when a child meets a long unfamiliar word in a book. A seam is a meaning unit, not a sound unit — scare | crow, not sca | recrow — so a child who has been dividing words into syllables has to switch from listening to thinking about what each piece means. The eight words are chosen so both halves are common: rain and bow, butter and cup, key and board. The teacher asks the child to say the two pieces after drawing the line; if the pieces are not both real words the line is in the wrong place, and the child can move it without erasing anything else.
G2-330.p3: The letters are large and widely spaced so the line has room, and the page prints on one sheet. It belongs after the picture-plus-picture base page, which has the child build the same kind of word from two pictures, and before the compound-detective page, where some of the printed words are not compounds at all. The word-web page then shows how one first word — rain — starts several compounds.

G2-331.h1: Match the Halves: Two Pictures, One Word
G2-331.title: Match the Halves Compound Words Worksheet – 2nd Grade | Free Printable PDF
G2-331.metaDescription: Match the halves: six first pictures in one column, six second pictures shuffled in another — draw a line from bird to house, then write birdhouse. Free 2nd grade PDF.
G2-331.p1: Two columns of pictures and a column of handwriting rules make up this 2nd grade compound-words page. The middle column holds the first halves — a bird, a sun, a rain cloud, the earth, a hand, a water bottle — each with a dot at its right edge; the right column holds the second halves in shuffled order — a bag, a melon, a worm, a house, a coat, a flower — each with a dot at its left. The child draws a line from each first picture to the picture that finishes its word, then writes the whole word on the rule beside the first picture: birdhouse, sunflower, raincoat, earthworm, handbag, watermelon. Six lines, six words, and every second picture is used once.
G2-331.p2: Matching before writing is the scaffold this page adds to the base compound page. There, the two pictures sit side by side and only the spelling is open; here the child has to test each first half against six candidates and hear which combination is a real word — sun and worm is not, sun and flower is. The shuffle is deliberate: no line runs straight across, so the choice is a meaning choice, not a position one. Writing the word after drawing the line closes the loop, and the rule sits on the same row as the first picture so the child can check the two halves while spelling. The teacher looks for lines that cross the column twice; that row was guessed.
G2-331.p3: It prints on one sheet in color, with a long rule per row. Use it between the picture-plus-picture base page and the split-the-compound page, especially for children who can build a compound when the halves are handed to them but cannot yet choose the halves. The compound-detective page follows for children who are ready to reject words that are not compounds.

G2-332.h1: Compound Detective: Which Six of Twelve Words Are Made of Two?
G2-332.title: Compound Detective Worksheet for 2nd Grade | Free Printable PDF
G2-332.metaDescription: Compound detective: twelve picture words — jellyfish, kitchen, keyboard, donkey — six are compounds. Circle those six and write their two parts. Free 2nd grade PDF.
G2-332.p1: Twelve picture-word cards sit in a dashed bank at the top of this 2nd grade compound-words page: kitchen, jellyfish, keyboard, bookshelf, necklace, donkey, pumpkin, earthworm, penguin, watermelon, potato, mushroom. Six of them are made of two words and six only look long. Under the bank are six numbered rows, each with two handwriting rules joined by a plus sign. The child circles the six compound words in the bank and writes the two parts of each one on a row: jelly + fish, key + board, book + shelf, neck + lace, earth + worm, water + melon. The other six — kitchen, donkey, pumpkin, penguin, potato, mushroom — stay uncircled.
G2-332.p2: Is it made of two words? is a harder question than it sounds, because long words all look the same on the page. A detective has to take the word apart and ask whether both pieces are real words that add up to the meaning: jelly and fish do, and a jellyfish is a fish-shaped jelly; don and key do not make a donkey. That test, rather than length or the presence of a familiar chunk, is what the page trains, and the six foils are chosen because they tempt — pumpkin, penguin and potato all begin with something that sounds like a word. The teacher asks for the two parts out loud before anything is circled; a child who cannot name two real parts has found a foil.
G2-332.p3: The page prints on one sheet and is finished when six rows are full and six bank words are untouched. It is the judgment face of the family: use it after the picture-plus-picture page and the split-the-compound page, where every word on the paper is a compound, and before the word-web page. Necklace and mushroom are the two cards that provoke the best classroom argument, and the answer key settles it.

G2-333.h1: Word Web: One Word, Many Compounds
G2-333.title: Compound Word Web Worksheet for 2nd Grade | Free Printable PDF
G2-333.metaDescription: Word web: one word in the middle, fish or rain, with three pictures branching off it. Write each new compound — starfish, raincoat, rainbow. Free 2nd grade PDF.
G2-333.p1: One word in the middle, three pictures around it, twice: this 2nd grade compound-words page prints two word webs. In the top card a boxed fish with the word fish printed under it sits at the left, and three branches lead to three picture equations — a goldfish plus a fish, a starfish plus a fish, a jellyfish plus a fish — each ending in a handwriting rule. In the bottom card the hub is a rain cloud labeled rain, and its three branches are a cloud plus a coat, a cloud plus a rainbow, a cloud plus a drop. The child writes the compound each branch makes on its rule: goldfish, starfish, jellyfish; raincoat, rainbow, raindrop. The hub word is printed; the branch words come from the pictures.
G2-333.p2: A web shows something the row-by-row pages cannot: one word is a building block that appears in many compounds, sometimes at the end (goldfish, starfish) and sometimes at the front (raincoat, rainbow). Seeing fish stay fixed while the first half changes teaches the child to read a compound as a head plus a modifier, and seeing rain move to the front of the next web shows the block can go either side. The hub word is given so the spelling of the repeated part is never in doubt; the effort goes into the changing half. The teacher asks, after the three rules are filled, for one more word with fish in it — catfish, swordfish — and the string keeps going off the page.
G2-333.p3: It prints on one sheet with three rules per web and generous space between the two. It closes the compound-words sequence: the picture-plus-picture page builds one word at a time, the split and match pages take words apart and put them together, and the web collects a family around one word. A dictionary page or a word wall is the natural next step for the words the class adds.

G2-317.title: Verb Forms Worksheet for 2nd Grade | Free Printable PDF
G2-317.metaDescription: Verb forms worksheet: a six-verb table with he/she today and yesterday columns — fill the gaps (dances, jumped, sang) — then finish three sentences. Free 2nd grade PDF.
G2-317.p1: A verb table takes up the top half of this 2nd grade verb-forms worksheet. Six pictured verbs run down the left — dance, read, jump, wander, run, sing — under two column headings, he/she today and yesterday. Four cells are filled in as models (danced, read, jumps, runs) and the other eight are dashed boxes for the child to complete: dances, reads, jumped, wanders, wandered, ran, sings, sang. Below the table are three picture sentences with a gap and the base verb in a chip at the end: Last night Mia ______ for an hour (dance). Anna ______ at the picnic yesterday (sing). Emma ______ every afternoon (read). The child fills the table, then uses it to finish the sentences.
G2-317.p2: The table is the point. English verbs change in two directions a second grader has to control at once — the -s of he and she today, and the -ed or the changed vowel of yesterday — and a table puts both on one line so the child can see that jump becomes jumps one way and jumped the other. The given cells are placed so every row has a model somewhere near it. The three sentences then ask for the same forms in use, where the time word (last night, every afternoon) tells the child which column to look in. The teacher watches the irregular rows: a child who writes singed or runned has learned the rule and not yet the exceptions, and the table shows exactly which.
G2-317.p3: It prints on one sheet with dashed answer boxes large enough for a second grader's writing. The match-the-past-form page is the recognition step before this, the choose-the-right-form page keeps the child circling rather than writing, and the irregular-verbs page does the same table for be, have, do and go.

G2-334.h1: Match the Verb to Its Past Form
G2-334.title: Match the Verb to Its Past Form – 2nd Grade | Free Printable PDF
G2-334.metaDescription: Match the verb to its past form: six verbs on the left, twelve chips on the right — ran, sang, jumped plus he/she forms as decoys. One line per verb. Free 2nd grade PDF.
G2-334.p1: Six verbs are stacked in cards down the left of this 2nd grade verb-forms page — sing, gather, jump, wander, dance, run — four of them with a small picture of a child doing the action. Down the right are twelve outlined chips: ran, wandered, danced, jumped, sang, runs, gathered, gathers, wanders, dances, jumps, sings. Only six of the chips are yesterday forms; the other six are he/she today forms put there as decoys. The child reads a verb, finds its past form on the right and draws a line to it — sing to sang, run to ran, gather to gathered — one line for each verb, and six chips are left unjoined.
G2-334.p2: Recognizing a past form is the first rung, and the decoys are what give the page its teaching value. A child who joins jump to jumps has found a form of the right verb but not the right form; the line looks plausible and is wrong, and that is the mistake this page exists to surface before the child has to write the forms. Two of the six verbs are irregular — sang, ran — so the child cannot simply look for -ed. The teacher checks the leftover chips: they should all end in -s, and a stray -ed chip left over means a line went to the wrong column of the table.
G2-334.p3: A pencil and one sheet; no writing at all. It is the first page of the verb-forms family in difficulty, before the today-and-yesterday table where the child writes the forms. The choose-the-right-form page keeps the recognition format but puts the forms under a sentence, and the find-the-verb page reverses the task — the past form is in the sentence and the child writes the base.

G2-335.h1: Verb Forms in Sentences with Pictures: Write the Form That Fits
G2-335.title: Verb Forms in Sentences Worksheet for 2nd Grade | Free Printable PDF
G2-335.metaDescription: Verb forms in sentences: six picture sentences, each with a gap and the base verb in a chip — Lily ___ in the garden today (read). Write the form. Free 2nd grade PDF.
G2-335.p1: No table, six sentences. This 2nd grade verb-forms page prints six picture sentence cards, one under another, each with a dashed gap and the base verb in an outlined chip at the end of the line: Lily ______ in the garden today (read). Today Ben ______ with his sister (run). On Mondays Anna ______ at the club (sing). Every day Mia ______ in the park (wander). Tom ______ at the pool yesterday (jump). After school Leo ______ at home (dance). A picture of a child reading, running, singing, walking with a backpack, jumping rope or dancing sits at the left of each card. The child reads the whole sentence, finds the time word, and writes the form that fits: reads, runs, sings, wanders, jumped, dances.
G2-335.p2: Choosing a form from a sentence is the skill the verb table was practicing for. The chip gives the child the verb so that nothing has to be recalled; the sentence gives the time — today, on Mondays, every day, yesterday, after school — and the child has to notice it and act on it. Five of the six sentences are present, which means the -s ending gets most of the work, and the one yesterday sentence checks that the child is actually reading the time word and not writing -s everywhere. The teacher covers the chip and asks the child to say the sentence with the form in it; if it sounds wrong aloud, it is wrong.
G2-335.p3: It prints on one sheet with wide dashed boxes. The base today-and-yesterday page combines a table with three sentences of this kind, so this face is the extension for a child who has the table down and needs more sentences. The choose-the-right-form page offers the same kind of sentences with three printed forms to circle, for a child not yet ready to write the ending unaided.

G2-336.h1: The Irregular Verbs: be, have, do, go — Today and Yesterday
G2-336.title: Irregular Verbs be, have, do, go – 2nd Grade | Free Printable PDF
G2-336.metaDescription: Irregular verbs be, have, do, go: a four-row table of he/she today and yesterday forms — write is, has, had, does, did, went — then three sentences. Free 2nd grade PDF.
G2-336.p1: Four verbs only, and the four that break every rule: this 2nd grade verb-forms page prints a table with go, have, be and do down the left and two columns, he/she today and yesterday. Two cells are given as anchors — goes and was — and six are dashed boxes: went, has, had, is, does, did. Under the table are three sentences with a gap and the base verb in a chip: Every morning Leo ______ to school (go). Yesterday Tom ______ at the zoo (be). Yesterday Lily ______ a bad cold (have). The child fills the table first, then uses it for the sentences. There are no pictures on this page; the verbs are too abstract to draw.
G2-336.p2: Be, have, do and go are the four verbs a child uses most and the four that no rule predicts — is and was share not a single letter with be. They are learned as a set, by memory and by hearing, which is why this page isolates them instead of mixing them into a table of regular verbs where a child could lean on -s and -ed. The two given cells are placed so a child who knows goes can find went by reading across, and a child who knows was can find is by reading back. The teacher reads the three sentences aloud with the child's answers in place; a wrong form of these verbs is the one a second grader can always hear.
G2-336.p3: One sheet, no pictures, large dashed boxes. Use it after the regular today-and-yesterday table so the child meets the rule before the exceptions, and keep it as a reference: the finished table is a small chart of the four verbs the child will need in every piece of writing. The find-the-verb page then asks the child to spot forms like went and was inside sentences and give back the base verb.

G2-337.h1: Choose the Right Verb Form: Circle One of Three
G2-337.title: Choose the Right Verb Form Worksheet for 2nd Grade | Free Printable PDF
G2-337.metaDescription: Choose the right verb form: eight sentences, three forms printed under each — sit, sits, sat — circle the one that fits the time word. Free printable 2nd grade PDF.
G2-337.p1: Eight sentence cards fill this 2nd grade verb-forms page, each with a dashed gap in the sentence and three outlined chips underneath: Yesterday Tom ______ at the zoo — sit, sits, sat. Emma ______ every afternoon — swims, swam, swim. On Mondays Anna ______ at the club — climbs, climb, climbed. Every day Mia ______ in the park — hopped, hops, hop. Yesterday Max ______ at the party — shouts, shouted, shout. Last week Leo ______ in the forest — wanders, wander, wandered. Today Ben ______ with his sister — runs, run, ran. Lily ______ in the garden today — dances, danced, dance. The last three cards carry a small picture. The child reads the sentence, finds the time word, and circles the form that fits. Nothing is written.
G2-337.p2: Three chips make this a choice between the base form, the he/she form and the past — the three forms the verb table teaches — with the wrong two always present as distractors. That is what makes circling harder than it looks: run is a real word and a real form, but Today Ben run with his sister is wrong, and a child has to hear the missing -s. The sentences are the same shape as the sentence pages in this family, so a child moves between circling and writing without meeting new sentence types. The teacher asks the child to read the sentence with the circled word in it, out loud, before moving on; the ear catches what the eye let through.
G2-337.p3: The page prints on one sheet with chips a second grader can circle cleanly. It is the recognition version of the verb-forms-in-sentences page: use it first for a child who is not yet ready to write the form, or afterward as a quick check. The match-the-past-form page is the other no-writing face, and the find-the-verb page moves from choosing a form to identifying one in a sentence.

G2-338.h1: Find the Verb, Write Its Base Form
G2-338.title: Find the Verb, Write Its Base Form – 2nd Grade | Free Printable PDF
G2-338.metaDescription: Find the verb: underline the verb in each of eight sentences — After school Leo dances at home — and write its base form, dance, in the dashed box. Free 2nd grade PDF.
G2-338.p1: Every sentence on this 2nd grade verb-forms page is complete — no gap, no chip. Eight of them are printed one to a card, six with a small picture at the left and each with a dashed box at the right: After school Leo dances at home. Yesterday Max jumped at the party. Last night Mia sang for an hour. Yesterday Tom shouted at the zoo. Today Ben reads with his sister. Last week Leo wandered in the forest. Anna ran at the picnic yesterday. Ben hides a red bike. The child underlines the verb in each sentence and writes its base form in the box: dance, jump, sing, shout, read, wander, run, hide. The forms in the sentences are a mix — -s endings, -ed endings and the irregular sang and ran.
G2-338.p2: Finding the verb is a word-class skill, and giving back its base form is a verb-forms skill; this page asks for both in one move, which is what a child does when looking a word up or when the teacher says use the verb jump. The sentences have exactly one verb each, and the surrounding words — names, times, places — are the same ones used across the family, so nothing distracts from the action word. Sang and ran are the rows that separate a child who is stripping -ed from a child who knows the verb: there is no ending to remove, only a vowel to change back. The teacher checks that the underline is on one word and that the box holds a word with no ending at all.
G2-338.p3: It prints on one sheet with a full dashed box per sentence. Use it last in the verb-forms sequence — after the table, the sentence pages and the choose-the-form page — because it assumes the child can already tell today from yesterday and now needs to travel from a form back to the verb. A nouns-and-verbs sort page is the companion for the underlining half of the task.

K-319.h1: Feelings: Match the Face to the Word
K-319.title: Feelings Worksheet for Kindergarten | Free Printable PDF
K-319.metaDescription: Feelings worksheet: six yellow faces on the left, six feeling words on the right; draw a line from each face to the word that names it. Free printable Kindergarten PDF.
K-319.p1: Six yellow faces run down the left of this Kindergarten feelings worksheet, each in its own white card: a wide grin, a worried frown, knitted brows over bared teeth, a gasp with wide eyes, a small round mouth of surprise, and heavy half-closed lids. Down the right sit six cream word cards in large type — surprised, scared, tired, happy, sad, angry — in an order that does not match the faces. A dot marks the inner edge of every card, and the child draws a line from each face to the one word that says how that face feels. Six faces, six words, every word used once.
K-319.p2: The child is reading a feeling off a face, not matching a noun to its object; the drawn features are the whole clue. Happy and sad come first for most five-year-olds. Angry is read from the brows, tired from the lids, and scared against surprised is the hardest pair on the page — both mouths are open, but the scared face has raised, fearful eyes and the surprised face a neat little o. The teacher asks the child to make each face before drawing the line: pulling the expression is what fixes the word.
K-319.p3: It prints on one sheet and needs only a pencil. This is the base page of the feelings family: the which-face-shows-the-feeling page turns the same six words into rows of three faces with one right answer, the how-do-you-feel page replaces the word with a pictured situation, and the draw-the-feeling-face page asks the child to produce the face rather than find it. Start here, then move in whichever direction the class needs.

K-331.h1: How Do You Feel? Circle the Face
K-331.title: How Do You Feel Worksheet for Kindergarten | Free Printable PDF
K-331.metaDescription: How do you feel: six pictured situations — a bed, a medal, a present, a storm — each over three faces; circle the face that fits. Free printable Kindergarten PDF.
K-331.p1: A picture stands at the top of each of the six numbered cards on this Kindergarten feelings page: a bed, a gold medal, red pajamas beside a crescent moon, a wrapped present, a storm cloud with lightning, and a syringe. Under each picture sit three yellow faces in small white tiles. The child looks at the picture, imagines being there, and circles the one face that shows how they would feel — tired at the bed, happy with the medal, scared of the storm. No feeling word is printed anywhere; the situation is the only prompt and the faces are the only answers.
K-331.p2: This is the inference step of the family. On the base page a word is given and a face found; here the child has to work out the feeling from a scene, which is the real-life version of the skill. Each card's three faces include the intended answer and two that do not fit, and across the page the same feeling never turns up on more than two cards, so a child cannot circle happy everywhere and be right. The teacher's question is the title itself, asked aloud at every card. A child who says scared at the syringe and another who says sad are both reasonable — that card is the one worth a conversation.
K-331.p3: One sheet, pencil or crayon, six circles to draw. The situations come from a fixed pool of everyday objects — the pool also holds a balloon, a teddy bear and a pillow under the moon — so the page reads the same way whichever six it shows. Follow it with the how-do-I-feel-today check-in, where the situation is the child's own morning, or go back to the match-the-face-to-the-word page if the faces themselves are still uncertain.

K-332.title: Draw the Feeling Face Worksheet for Kindergarten | Free Printable PDF
K-332.metaDescription: Draw the feeling face: four cards, one word each — scared, angry, happy, sad — over an empty circle; draw the face that shows it. Free printable Kindergarten PDF.
K-332.p1: Four big cream cards fill this Kindergarten page, two across and two down, and each holds nothing but a feeling word in large teal type and an empty circle beneath it: scared, angry, happy, sad. There are no printed faces to copy. The child reads the word and draws, inside the circle, a face that shows that feeling — the mouth, the eyes, the brows. The circles are wide enough for a whole hand's drawing, and the four words are the four feelings a five-year-old can draw apart from one another.
K-332.p2: Producing a face is a different skill from recognising one. On the matching pages of the feelings family the child points at what an artist drew; here they must decide what angry looks like and put it on paper, which means thinking about which features change. Most children get happy and sad from the mouth alone. Angry needs the brows to slope inward and scared needs the eyes to open wide, and a child who draws the same round-mouth face for both has found the exact thing to talk about. Ask them to make the face in a mirror first and then draw what they see.
K-332.p3: Print one per child; crayons work better than pencil here because the circles are large. The page has no answer key by design — any face that reads as the word is right. Use it after the match-the-face-to-the-word page, and pair it with the how-do-I-feel-today page, where the same drawing circle appears once and the feeling is the child's own.

K-333.h1: Feels Good or Feels Bad? Sort the Faces
K-333.title: Feels Good or Feels Bad Worksheet for Kindergarten | Free Printable PDF
K-333.metaDescription: Feels good or feels bad: six yellow faces across the top, two labelled boxes below; draw a line from each face to the box its feeling belongs in. Free Kindergarten PDF.
K-333.p1: A single row of six yellow faces runs across the top of this Kindergarten sorting page, each in a small cream card with an orange dot beneath it. At the bottom sit two large boxes with dashed tops, labelled Feels good and Feels bad. The child draws a line from every face down into the box where that feeling belongs: the grin, the laugh and the calm smile go one way, the frightened face, the sad frown and the wincing face go the other. No feeling word is printed on the page, and three faces belong in each box.
K-333.p2: This page asks about valence, not vocabulary: not what the feeling is called, but whether it is comfortable or uncomfortable to have. That is why faces the word pages leave out can appear here — a laughing face or a wince does not need a name to be sorted. It is also why a child who cannot yet read any of the feelings words can complete the page alone. The interesting ground is the middle: the teacher listens for a child saying that a face could go either way, and asks why.
K-333.p3: It prints on one sheet; a pencil and a ruler make the six lines tidy but neither is essential. The page is the odd one of its family — every sibling works with a feeling word, and this one works with the feeling itself. Use it first with children who are not yet reading, then go to the match-the-face-to-the-word page once the good and bad sides are secure.

K-334.title: Which Face Shows the Feeling – Kindergarten | Free Printable PDF
K-334.metaDescription: Which face shows the feeling: six rows, one word on the left — tired, angry, happy, scared — three faces on the right; circle the one that matches. Free Kindergarten PDF.
K-334.p1: Six wide rows stack down this Kindergarten page. On the left of each row a feeling word sits alone in large type — tired, angry, happy, scared, surprised, sad — and on the right stand three yellow faces in white tiles. Only one of the three shows the word; the child reads the word and circles that face. The other two faces are real feelings too, taken from the same six, so the wrong choices look as plausible as the right one. Nothing is written; six circles finish the page.
K-334.p2: The difference from the base matching page is that there is no elimination. With six faces and six words the last pair falls into place by itself; here each row is its own question with a fresh set of three, and a child must actually read scared and find the frightened face. The two faces easiest to confuse — scared and surprised — are kept out of the same row, so a row tests recognition rather than a fine distinction. The teacher can cover the faces, ask the child to say the word and make the face, then uncover and circle.
K-334.p3: One sheet, pencil or crayon. This is the quick-check page of the feelings family: six answers, one look, and the teacher knows which of the six words are secure. Move to the how-do-you-feel page when all six are, since that page drops the word and gives a situation instead; go back to the match-the-face-to-the-word page if two or more rows go wrong.

K-335.title: How Do I Feel Today Worksheet for Kindergarten | Free Printable PDF
K-335.metaDescription: How do I feel today: circle one of six labelled faces, draw your own face in the circle, finish the line that starts with because. A check-in. Free Kindergarten PDF.
K-335.p1: The top band of this Kindergarten check-in page reads Today I feel… above a strip of six labelled faces: happy, sad, angry, scared, surprised, tired, each face with its word beneath it. Below is a large panel headed Draw your face with a single empty circle, and at the foot a lined box whose first handwriting rule begins with the word because. The child circles the face that fits their morning, draws their own face in the circle, and — with help, or in their own spelling — finishes the because line.
K-335.p2: There is no right answer on this page, which is the point. Every other page in the feelings family checks whether the child can read a feeling; this one asks them to report one, and the because line asks for a reason, which is the beginning of talking about feelings rather than only naming them. The six labelled faces double as a word wall, so a child who circles sad has the word in front of them when they draw. Teachers who run a morning check-in can use the same sheet every day and watch what changes.
K-335.p3: It prints on one sheet; the two writing rules at the bottom are full three-line handwriting guides, so a child who dictates to an adult can copy the sentence underneath. Keep the finished sheets — a week of them makes a small record for a parent meeting. The draw-the-feeling-face page practises the drawing on its own with four given words, and the base match-the-face-to-the-word page is where the six labels come from.

G2-318.title: Animal Fact File Worksheet for 2nd Grade | Free Printable PDF
G2-318.metaDescription: Animal fact file: a forest creature, a box to draw where it lives, six blank rows — group, home, food, legs, covering, can it fly — and a starter. Free 2nd grade PDF.
G2-318.p1: One forest creature fills this 2nd grade animal fact file — on the printed sheet it is a hedgehog, its name in a banner beside the picture. To the right of the picture is a dashed box labelled Draw where it lives. Below runs the file itself: six rows with a heading on the left and three-line handwriting rules on the right — Animal group, Where it lives, What it eats, Legs, Body covering and Can it fly? The last band gives a sentence starter, The hedgehog can, with a rule to finish it. Every fact row is blank; the child finds out and writes.
G2-318.p2: This is a research page, not a comprehension page: nothing on the sheet tells the child what a hedgehog eats. The six headings are the questions, and the child answers them from a class book, a short film or the teacher's own reading aloud, one short fact per row. The headings are the same six fields for every animal in the family, which is what makes the file a template — a child who has done the hedgehog can do a fox or an owl with the same page. The drawing box asks for the habitat, not the animal, so the child has to decide what a hedgehog's home looks like.
G2-318.p3: Print one per child, or one per group with the animal chosen for them. This is the base page of the animal-fact-file family, and it owns the empty template; the word-bank page prints the six true facts in a bank to copy from, the circle-the-true-facts page turns each row into three choices, and the write-three-sentences page prints the file filled in and asks for sentences instead. Use this one when the class has a source to read.

G2-339.h1: Animal Fact File: Circle the True Facts
G2-339.title: Circle the True Facts Animal Worksheet for 2nd Grade | Free Printable PDF
G2-339.metaDescription: Circle the true facts: six fact rows, each with three choices — mammal, bird, insect; air, land, water — circle the one true for this animal. Free 2nd grade PDF.
G2-339.p1: Every row of the fact file on this 2nd grade page is already filled — three times over. Beside Animal group the chips read mammal, bird, insect; beside Where it lives, air, land, water; beside What it eats, plants, meat, both; beside Legs, three numerals; beside Body covering, shell, spines, fur; and beside Can it fly?, no and yes. The child reads the three choices in each row and circles the one that is true for the forest creature pictured at the top, which on the printed sheet is a hedgehog. Then they draw its home in the dashed box and finish The hedgehog can.
G2-339.p2: Circling replaces writing here, and that changes who the page is for. A child who knows that a hedgehog has spines but cannot yet spell spines can still show it, and a child who has never met the animal can reason from the picture — it clearly has legs, it clearly has no wings. The wrong choices are true of other animals in the same theme, not nonsense, so the Body covering row really does ask the child to weigh shell against spines against fur. Across the page the correct chip sits in every position, so no column is the answer column.
G2-339.p3: It prints on one sheet. This is the recognition face of the animal-fact-file family and carries no writing standard — it is a science page about what an animal is, where it lives and how it is covered. Use it before the base page, where the same six rows are blank, or as the check afterwards; the word-bank page sits between the two, with the true facts printed but mixed among decoys.

G2-340.h1: Animal Fact File with a Word Bank
G2-340.title: Animal Fact File with a Word Bank for 2nd Grade | Free Printable PDF
G2-340.metaDescription: Animal fact file with a word bank: ten words — six true facts and four decoys — to copy into the right rows of a blank six-row fact file. Free printable 2nd grade PDF.
G2-340.p1: A dashed word bank sits where the drawing box would be on this 2nd grade fact file, holding ten chips in two rows: mammal, fish, land, both, 8, 0, fur, no, 4, spines. Six of them are true of the forest creature at the top — on the printed sheet a hedgehog — and four are decoys drawn from the same fields. Below is the six-row file with its three-line writing rules, Animal group down to Can it fly?, every row blank. The child finds the true fact for each row in the bank and copies it in, then finishes the sentence starter, The hedgehog can, at the bottom.
G2-340.p2: Copying from a bank is the scaffold between circling and writing: the child still has to select — fish or mammal, fur or spines, 4 legs or 8 — but the spelling is supplied. The four decoys come from at least two different fields, so a child cannot finish by dropping the leftovers wherever a row is empty; each decoy belongs to the same row as a true chip and has to be ruled out there. It is a good page for a child who knows the animal but freezes at a blank line, and for a class where spelling is not the lesson.
G2-340.p3: One sheet, pencil, ten words to weigh. The base animal fact file page has the same six rows and no bank, so it is the natural next step; the circle-the-true-facts page is the one before, where the choices sit inside each row and nothing is written. The write-three-sentences page uses a completed file as its source instead.

G2-341.h1: Animal Fact File: Write Three Sentences
G2-341.title: Animal Fact File: Write Three Sentences – 2nd Grade | Free Printable PDF
G2-341.metaDescription: Write three sentences: a completed fact file is printed beside the animal; finish The hedgehog is, has, eats from it and add one fact of your own. Free 2nd grade PDF.
G2-341.p1: The fact file on this 2nd grade page comes already filled in. Beside the picture of the forest creature — a hedgehog on the printed sheet — a compact six-row table reads mammal, land, both, 4, spines, no against its headings. Beneath, a lined panel headed Write three sentences about the animal offers three starters, each on its own two-line handwriting rule: The hedgehog is, The hedgehog has, The hedgehog eats. A fourth pair of rules at the bottom has no starter at all. The child reads the file, turns three of its facts into three sentences, and adds one more fact of their own on the last lines.
G2-341.p2: The move here is from fact to sentence. Is, has and eats point at three different rows — group or covering, legs or spines, food — and the child has to choose which fact fits which verb, then write it out as a complete sentence with a capital and a full stop. The open fourth line is where a child who knows something the file does not say — it curls into a ball, it sleeps all winter — gets to write it. There is no drawing box on this page; the space goes to the writing rules, which are two lines each so a real 2nd grade sentence can wrap.
G2-341.p3: Print one per child. This is the composing page of the animal-fact-file family and the only one that supplies the facts in full, which makes it the right page for a writing lesson rather than a research one. The base page reverses it — six blank rows and a source to read — and the compare-two-animals page puts two printed files side by side.

G2-342.h1: Compare Two Animals: Same and Different
G2-342.title: Compare Two Animals Worksheet for 2nd Grade | Free Printable PDF
G2-342.metaDescription: Compare two animals: two printed fact files side by side; circle same or different for group, home, food and covering, then write two of each. Free 2nd grade PDF.
G2-342.p1: Two forest creatures share this 2nd grade page, each in its own card with a picture, a name banner and a printed four-row file: Animal group, Where it lives, What it eats, Body covering. On the sheet shown they are a ladybug and an eagle — insect and bird, both listed in the air, both eating meat, shell against feathers. Beneath the cards sit four small rows, one per fact, each with a same chip and a different chip to circle. The bottom panel has four handwriting rules with starters: Same, Same, Different, Different. The child reads both files, circles four times, then writes two likenesses and two differences as sentences.
G2-342.p2: The pair is chosen so that exactly two of the four facts agree, which is what makes the writing panel work — there are always two sames and two differents to find, never three of one. A child who circles by looking at the pictures will get the covering right and the food wrong; the files have to be read. The legs and can-it-fly rows from the base file are dropped here because they are trivial to compare, leaving the four facts that ask for a real look.
G2-342.p3: One sheet, no drawing. This face fans out by theme rather than by animal — the two animals come from the wave's theme and the page never names them in its title, since a title would give the comparison away. It is the family's only two-animal page; the write-three-sentences page is the one-animal composing step before it, and the who-am-I page uses the same fact fields as clues.

G2-343.title: Who Am I Mystery Animal Worksheet for 2nd Grade | Free Printable PDF
G2-343.metaDescription: Who am I: a picture bank of six named animals and three riddle cards with five first-person clues each; find the animal, write its name and draw it. Free 2nd grade PDF.
G2-343.p1: A dashed picture bank runs across the top of this 2nd grade page with six small forest creatures, each named under its picture — on the printed sheet a bear, a lizard, an ant, a bat, a wolf and an eagle. Under it are three tall riddle cards. Each begins Who am I? and gives five clues in the first person: I live on land. I eat plants and meat. I have fur. I cannot fly. I can swim. To the right of the clues is a Name line, and beyond it a dashed box to draw the answer. The child reads the five clues, finds the one animal in the bank they all fit, writes its name and draws it.
G2-343.p2: Each card's five clues rule out every other animal in the bank, and the bank holds three extra animals that are not the answer to any card, so the last riddle cannot be solved by elimination alone. The clues are the fact-file fields turned into sentences — group, home, food, covering, legs, flying, swimming — which is why a child who has done the base fact file recognises the shape at once. Reading for the one detail that separates the bear from the wolf, I eat plants and meat, is the informational-reading skill the page is built on.
G2-343.p3: It prints on one sheet; the drawing boxes are small, so a pencil sketch is enough. This is the reading face of the animal-fact-file family and the only one that starts from text rather than from a picture. The six-animal bank is drawn from the wave's forest theme, and the page never names the answers in its title. Use it after the fact files have been written, when the fields are familiar.

G1-310.h1: Hundreds Chart Puzzle Pieces: Fill In the Numbers
G1-310.title: Hundreds Chart Puzzles Worksheet for 1st Grade | Free Printable PDF
G1-310.metaDescription: Hundreds chart puzzles: six loose pieces of the 100 chart, one number printed on each; fill every empty cell by going 1 sideways or 10 up and down. Free 1st grade PDF.
G1-310.p1: Six puzzle pieces sit on this 1st grade page, each in its own card, as if cut out of a hundreds chart with scissors: two 3-by-3 squares, an L, a plus sign and two T shapes. One cell on each piece is shaded and carries a printed number — 76, 62, 22, 17, 50, 89 on the sheet shown — and every other cell is empty with a dashed inner edge. The child writes every missing number by moving from the printed one: 1 more to the right, 1 less to the left, 10 more below, 10 less above. No chart is printed; the piece is all there is.
G1-310.p2: The page works because the printed number can sit anywhere on the piece — in a corner, in the middle, at the end of an arm — so the child has to move both ways from it, sometimes two steps in a row, and sometimes down first and then across. That is the mental hundreds chart the 1st grade base-ten work asks for: 10 more and 10 less found without counting, read straight off the place the number holds. A piece whose numbers cross a ten — 89 to 90, 50 to 49 — is the one to watch, since a child who writes 80 above 89 has moved a column instead of a row.
G1-310.p3: One sheet, pencil, some thirty numbers to write. This is the base page of the hundreds-chart-puzzles family and the plain fill-the-piece task; the where-does-the-piece-go page reverses it and asks where a fully printed piece belongs on an empty chart, and the find-the-wrong-number page prints the pieces filled with one error each. A hundreds chart on the wall is the only support the page needs.

G1-347.title: Where Does the Piece Go Worksheet for 1st Grade | Free Printable PDF
G1-347.metaDescription: Where does the piece go: a 100 chart with only its top row and left column printed, and four numbered pieces; find each piece's place and write it in. Free 1st grade PDF.
G1-347.p1: An almost empty hundreds chart fills the top of this 1st grade page. Only its edges are printed: 1 to 10 across the top row and 11, 21, 31 down to 91 down the left column, with eighty-one blank cells between them. Under the chart lie four puzzle pieces, every cell already numbered — a plus with 38 at its centre, an S of 16, 25, 26, 35, a T carrying 24 and 32 to 34, and an L reading 64, 65, 66 down to 84. The child reads each piece, works out where it sits on the chart, and writes its numbers into the right cells. Nothing else is written.
G1-347.p2: The task is the reverse of the base puzzle-pieces page. There the child builds numbers out from one; here the numbers are given and the child has to find the position, which means reading a number as a row and a column — 38 is in the row that starts with 31, in the eighth column — and then checking that the rest of the piece lands where it should. The printed edges are the guides: a child places 64 by sliding down the left column to 61 and across to the fourth cell. A piece put one row too high shows at once, because its other numbers stop fitting.
G1-347.p3: It prints on one sheet; a ruler helps keep the writing inside the small cells. Use this page after the base fill-in-the-numbers page, when the child can move on a piece and needs to see how the pieces relate to the whole chart. The jump-puzzles page takes the same moves off the chart altogether and turns them into arrow chains.

G2-321.title: Jump Puzzles Hundreds Chart Worksheet for 2nd Grade | Free Printable PDF
G2-321.metaDescription: Jump puzzles: eight cards, a start number and three arrows each — up is 10 less, down 10 more, left 1 less, right 1 more; write where you land. Free 2nd grade PDF.
G2-321.p1: A key across the top of this 2nd grade page fixes the four moves: an up arrow is −10, down is +10, left is −1, right is +1. Below it are eight numbered cards, and each is a chain — a shaded start number, three arrow tiles in a row, a pointer, and a dashed box at the end. Start at 30, go left, down, left, and write where you land; start at 98, go up, right, right. The start numbers on the sheet run from 2 to 98, so some chains cross a ten and some sit right at the edge of the chart in the child's head. No chart is printed; the child holds it in mind.
G2-321.p2: Three moves in a row is what separates this from a single 10-more-or-10-less question. The child has to keep a running position — 30, then 29, then 39, then 38 — and the arrows never double back on themselves, so no move undoes the one before and the answer is always a different square from the start. The moves mix ones and tens in one chain, which is exactly the 2nd grade mental arithmetic of adding and subtracting 10 and 1: 44 up, up, right is 44 − 10 − 10 + 1 without ever writing the sum.
G2-321.p3: One sheet, eight answers, no working space needed beyond the box. This page is the chain-of-moves face of the hundreds-chart-puzzles family; the mystery-number page uses the same arrow key but points two arrows at one square, and the how-far-apart page asks the child to count the jumps between two numbers instead of following them. A wall chart lets a struggling child trace each chain with a finger.

G2-322.h1: Mystery Number: Two Arrows, One Square
G2-322.title: Mystery Number Hundreds Chart Worksheet for 2nd Grade | Free Printable PDF
G2-322.metaDescription: Mystery number: eight cards, two numbers and two arrows that point to one square of the hundreds chart — 24 down and 33 right both reach 34; write it. Free 2nd grade PDF.
G2-322.p1: Each of the eight cards on this 2nd grade page holds two shaded numbers stacked one above the other, an arrow beside each, and a single dashed box that both arrows point into. On the sheet shown the first card reads 24 with a down arrow and 33 with a right arrow: 10 more than 24 is 34, 1 more than 33 is 34, and 34 is the mystery number. The arrow key at the top — up −10, down +10, left −1, right +1 — is the only text. One clue is always a move of 10 and the other a move of 1, and the child writes the one number both clues reach.
G2-322.p2: Two arrows meeting at one square make the page self-checking, which is why it works as an independent task: if the child's two moves give two different numbers, one of them is wrong, and they know it before the teacher does. The two-clue shape also lets a child who is unsure of one move use the other — a child who cannot yet do 10 more than 24 can do 1 more than 33 and then see what 24 down must be. The cards are wordless apart from the key, so the page reads the same in any classroom.
G2-322.p3: It prints on one sheet with eight boxes to fill. This is the riddle face of the hundreds-chart-puzzles family: the jump-puzzles page chains three moves from one start instead, and the base puzzle-pieces page does the same 10-and-1 moves on a cut-out piece. Use the mystery page when children can do the moves and you want them to check their own work.

G1-348.h1: Find the Wrong Number on the Piece
G1-348.title: Find the Wrong Number Worksheet for 1st Grade | Free Printable PDF
G1-348.metaDescription: Find the wrong number: six hundreds chart pieces, every cell printed and exactly one wrong on each; circle it and write the right number in the box. Free 1st grade PDF.
G1-348.p1: Six fully printed puzzle pieces sit on this 1st grade page — a plus, two L shapes, a 3-by-3 square and two T shapes — and every one of them contains a single mistake. On the sheet shown the plus reads 39, 84, 49, 50, 59, and 84 sits where 48 belongs; the square runs 2, 3, 4, 12, 13, 14, 22, 23, 33, and the last cell should be 24. A dashed box waits beside each piece. The child finds the number that does not fit the chart, circles it, and writes the right number in the box. There are no clean pieces; every piece has exactly one error.
G1-348.p2: Checking is a different act from filling. On the base page the child produces numbers; here they have to read six that are already there and decide which one breaks the pattern, which means testing each cell against its neighbours — is this 1 more than the cell to its left, is it 10 more than the cell above. The errors are the ones children actually make: digits swapped, a 10 written where a 1 belongs, a column jumped. Because the rest of the piece is right, the wrong cell is provable from the cells around it, and a child who circles the wrong one can be shown why.
G1-348.p3: One sheet, six circles and six corrections. This is the error-hunt face of the hundreds-chart-puzzles family and the one to give after the base fill-in-the-numbers page, when children make the moves confidently and need to start checking them. The where-does-the-piece-go page uses the same kind of printed pieces but asks for their place on an empty chart.

G2-323.h1: How Far Apart? Count the Jumps
G2-323.title: How Far Apart Hundreds Chart Worksheet for 2nd Grade | Free Printable PDF
G2-323.metaDescription: How far apart: eight pairs of numbers — 4 to 35, 63 to 86 — with a down counter and a right counter under each; write how many jumps of 10 and of 1. Free 2nd grade PDF.
G2-323.p1: Eight cards on this 2nd grade page each show two shaded numbers joined by an orange pointer — 4 to 35, 11 to 22, 24 to 67, 63 to 86, 13 to 78, 87 to 99, 85 to 96, 6 to 47 on the sheet shown. Under the pair sit two small counters: a down arrow with a dashed box, and a right arrow with a dashed box. The child works out how many jumps of 10 down and how many jumps of 1 right carry the first number to the second, and writes the two counts. From 4 to 35 is three down and one right; from 63 to 86, two down and three right.
G2-323.p2: This is distance on the chart, measured in moves rather than subtracted. The second number is always below and to the right of the first, so both counts are positive and each runs from 1 to 6 — no card asks for zero jumps in either direction, and none needs more than six. What the child is really doing is splitting a difference into tens and ones — 35 − 4 = 31 = three tens and one — but the page never shows a subtraction, and a child who has not met the column method can still count their way there on a wall chart.
G2-323.p3: It prints on one sheet with sixteen small boxes. This face closes the hundreds-chart-puzzles family: the jump-puzzles page gives the moves and asks for the landing, and this page gives the landing and asks for the moves. Use it once the arrow key on the jump page is automatic, and ask the child to say the two counts as a sum afterwards.

G3-377.h1: Division with Remainders: Ring the Groups
G3-377.title: Division with Remainders Worksheet for 3rd Grade | Free Printable PDF
G3-377.metaDescription: Division with remainders: four piles of animal pictures — 29 elephants ÷ 3 — ring groups of the divisor, write how many groups and how many are left. Free 3rd grade PDF.
G3-377.p1: Four piles of small animal pictures run down this 3rd grade page, each in its own card with the division written beside it: 29 ÷ 3 over twenty-nine elephants, 25 ÷ 2 over twenty-five zebras, 9 ÷ 2 over nine cats, 14 ÷ 5 over fourteen ducklings. Under each division wait two dashed boxes, the second marked R. The child draws rings around groups of the divisor — threes in the elephants, twos in the zebras — counts the rings, and writes that count in the first box and the pictures left outside any ring in the second. Every pile on the page leaves something over.
G3-377.p2: The remainder is a picture before it is a number here: the two elephants standing outside the rings are the 2 in 9 R 2. That is the concrete step the family builds on, and it is why the pictures are in neat rows of ten — a child can ring across a row and see how many threes fit. The divisors on the sheet are 2, 3 and 5 and the piles run up to 29, so a child who knows the twos, threes and fives tables can predict the rings before drawing them; a child who does not can still get every answer by ringing. Notation and picture agree on every card.
G3-377.p3: One sheet, a pencil for the rings and the boxes. This is the base page of the division-with-remainders family and the only one with a pile to ring; the share-it-out page deals the same kind of pile into boxes instead, and the practice-rows page keeps only the notation. The divisor set fans across the family — 2 to 5 on this sheet — so a class can start on small tables and move up. The standard is the 4th grade one, met here as 3rd grade practice.

G3-380.h1: Share It Out: What Is Left Over?
G3-380.title: Share It Out Division Worksheet for 3rd Grade | Free Printable PDF
G3-380.metaDescription: Share it out: four piles of fruit — 17 pomegranates into 3 boxes — and a dashed left-over box; deal one at a time, write each share and the remainder. Free 3rd grade PDF.
G3-380.p1: Fruit pictures fill the four cards of this 3rd grade sharing page: seventeen pomegranates, twenty lemons, fifteen blueberries and nine cherries, each pile with its division printed beside it — 17 ÷ 3, 20 ÷ 3, 15 ÷ 2, 9 ÷ 4. Under each pile stands a row of empty white boxes, as many as the divisor, and at the end of the row a smaller dashed box labelled left over. The child deals the pile out one picture at a time, a tally in each box in turn, until there are too few left to give every box one more; those go in the left-over box. Then they write how many each box got and the remainder, R.
G3-380.p2: This is sharing rather than grouping — the other way to read the same division. On the base page 17 ÷ 3 is how many threes fit in 17; here it is 17 fruits shared between 3 boxes, and the answer is what one box holds. Both give 5 R 2, and putting the two pages side by side is the clearest way to show it. The dashed left-over box is the point of the page: the remainder has a home, it is the fruit that could not be shared, and a child who tries to squeeze a sixth fruit into one box has found out what the remainder means.
G3-380.p3: One sheet; the piles stay under twenty so the dealing does not drag, and the divisors are 2, 3 and 4 on this sheet. The page carries the family's fruits theme where the base page carries animals. Follow it with the practice-rows page once the boxes are no longer needed, and use the number-line page for children who see sharing more easily as hopping back.

G3-381.title: Division with Remainders Practice Rows – 3rd Grade | Free Printable PDF
G3-381.metaDescription: Division with remainders practice: ten rows inside the 2 to 5 tables — 28 ÷ 5, 39 ÷ 4 — every one with a remainder; write the answer and the R. Free 3rd grade PDF.
G3-381.p1: Ten division facts sit in ten cards on this 3rd grade practice page, two across and five down, with no pictures at all: 28 ÷ 5, 9 ÷ 2, 25 ÷ 3, 39 ÷ 4, 22 ÷ 3, 19 ÷ 2, 11 ÷ 2, 37 ÷ 5, 29 ÷ 3, 53 ÷ 5. After each equals sign wait two dashed boxes, the second marked R. The child writes the quotient in the first and the remainder in the second. Every row on the page leaves something over — no division comes out exactly — and the divisors are the 2, 3, 4 and 5 tables, with the quotient never above 10.
G3-381.p2: Fluency is the whole job here. The child needs to find the largest multiple of the divisor that fits — the 5 in 28 ÷ 5 is 25 — and then count what is left, and to do it ten times without a picture to lean on. Because every row has a remainder, a child cannot fall back on the times-table answer; 25 ÷ 3 is not 8, it is 8 R 1. The page mixes the divisors so the child changes table row by row, and no divisor appears more than three times, so the fives cannot be done as a block.
G3-381.p3: It prints on one sheet with room for working beside each card. This is the notation-only face of the division-with-remainders family and the one to use after the ring-the-groups and share-it-out pages have made the remainder concrete. The exact-or-not page is the next step — it mixes in divisions that do come out exactly and asks the child to tell which.

G3-382.h1: Exact or Not? Divisions With and Without a Remainder
G3-382.title: Exact or Not Division Worksheet for 3rd Grade | Free Printable PDF
G3-382.metaDescription: Exact or not: eight divisions, half of them exact — 12 ÷ 2, 31 ÷ 4 — circle exact or remainder under each, then write the answer and R, 0 if exact. Free 3rd grade PDF.
G3-382.p1: Eight cards on this 3rd grade page each carry one division — 12 ÷ 2, 50 ÷ 5, 31 ÷ 4, 21 ÷ 2, 20 ÷ 4, 18 ÷ 3, 32 ÷ 3, 23 ÷ 4 on the sheet shown — followed by two dashed boxes, the second marked R, and under them two pill-shaped chips reading exact and remainder. The child decides whether the division comes out exactly, circles the right chip, and then fills both boxes, writing 0 in the R box when nothing is left. Four of the eight are exact and four are not, and they are mixed, so the chip has to be earned card by card.
G3-382.p2: Deciding is the skill on this page, and it is the one the practice-rows page cannot test, because there every row has a remainder. Here 20 ÷ 4 sits next to 21 ÷ 2, and the child has to ask of each whether the dividend is in the table — is 31 a multiple of 4, is 18 a multiple of 3. Writing R 0 for the exact ones keeps the notation the same across the page and stops the idea that a remainder is something only some divisions have. Divisors stay inside 2 to 5 and every quotient stays at 10 or below.
G3-382.p3: One sheet, eight decisions and sixteen boxes. This is the decision face of the division-with-remainders family, and the boundary is written into its title: half of these divisions come out exactly, and telling which is the task. Use it after the practice-rows page, and before the find-the-error page, where the child checks division that has already been done.

G3-383.h1: Find the Error: The Remainder Is Too Big
G3-383.title: Find the Error Division Worksheet for 3rd Grade | Free Printable PDF
G3-383.metaDescription: Find the error: eight divisions worked out with a remainder bigger than the divisor — 39 ÷ 5 = 6 R 9; cross it out, write the right answer and R. Free 3rd grade PDF.
G3-383.p1: Every division on this 3rd grade page has already been answered, in orange, and every answer is wrong in the same way: 39 ÷ 5 = 6 R 9, 10 ÷ 4 = 1 R 6, 26 ÷ 4 = 5 R 6, 42 ÷ 5 = 7 R 7, and four more. Under each printed pair sit two empty dashed boxes. The child crosses out the wrong quotient and remainder and writes the right ones beneath — 39 ÷ 5 is 7 R 4, not 6 R 9. The printed answers are not random: six fives and 9 really do make 39. The mistake is that 9 is bigger than 5, so another group of five could still have been taken.
G3-383.p2: A remainder that is larger than the divisor is the single most common division error at this stage, and this page is built from nothing else. Each wrong answer checks out by multiplication, which is why a child who only tests quotient times divisor plus remainder will find nothing wrong; they have to apply the second rule, that the remainder must be smaller than the divisor. Writing the correction underneath — one more group, a smaller remainder — is the whole lesson in two boxes.
G3-383.p3: One sheet, eight corrections. This is the checking face of the division-with-remainders family, and it belongs after the practice-rows and exact-or-not pages, when a child can produce answers and needs to learn to doubt them. The divisors stay small — 2 to 5 on this sheet — so the argument is always about the remainder, never about the table.

G3-384.h1: Hop Back on the Number Line: What Is Left?
G3-384.title: Hop Back Number Line Division Worksheet for 3rd Grade | Free Printable PDF
G3-384.metaDescription: Hop back on the number line: three lines with a dot at 15, 22 and 10; draw equal hops back until a whole hop no longer fits, write hops and landing. Free 3rd grade PDF.
G3-384.p1: Three number lines stretch across this 3rd grade page, one per card, each starting at 0 and marked every unit with the fives labelled. A teal dot sits on each line at the dividend — 15 on a line to 20, 22 on a line to 25, 10 on a line to 15 — and the division is printed beneath: 15 ÷ 4, 22 ÷ 3, 10 ÷ 3, each followed by a box and an R box. No hops are drawn. The child starts at the dot and draws hops back of the divisor's size — fours from 15 — until a whole hop would go past 0, then writes how many hops they drew and the number they landed on.
G3-384.p2: The number line makes the remainder a place rather than a count: hopping back three fours from 15 lands on 3, and 3 is where you stop because a fourth hop would need four more than you have. That is a different picture from rings on a pile, and for some children a clearer one, because the leftover is visible as the gap between the landing point and 0. Drawing the hops themselves, rather than reading printed ones, is what makes the page a division page — the child chooses the hop size from the divisor and keeps it constant.
G3-384.p3: One sheet, three lines, six boxes; the lines are long enough for hops of 2 to 5 without crowding. This is the measurement face of the division-with-remainders family, the dividends kept between 10 and 30 so the hops stay countable. Use it beside the ring-the-groups page to show the two pictures of one division, and before the practice-rows page.

K-320.title: Ordinal Numbers Worksheet for Kindergarten | Free Printable PDF
K-320.metaDescription: Ordinal numbers: three lines of seven animals behind a flag, two chips under each — 5th, circle; 6th, cross — count from the flag, mark the place. Free Kindergarten PDF.
K-320.p1: Three strips run down this Kindergarten ordinal numbers page, and each starts with a small orange flag at the left end of an arrow that runs above a line of seven animals — a raccoon, a gazelle, a camel, a hippo, a cat, a sheep and a tiger in the first line on the sheet shown. Under every animal is a grey dot. Below each line sit two chips: an ordinal number and a mark — 5th with a circle, 6th with a cross. The child starts at the flag, counts along to the place on the chip, and makes that mark on the animal standing there. Six marks finish the page.
K-320.p2: The flag is the whole idea. An ordinal only means something once you know where counting starts, and the flag fixes it at the left every time on this page, so the child's job is to count 1st, 2nd, 3rd along the row and stop at the right one. Two chips per line, each with its own mark, keep the child from guessing — a circle on the fifth animal and a cross on the sixth are two separate counts, and the chips reach 6th and 7th as well as 1st. The animals are all different, so the marked one can be named aloud afterwards: the cat is 5th.
K-320.p3: It prints on one sheet and needs only a pencil. This is the base page of the ordinal-numbers family and the Kindergarten page with the flag always on the left; the from-either-end page moves the flag to the right on some lines, and the three 1st grade pages ask the child to write the ordinal, read it as a word, or work it out from a picture. Say the ordinal aloud with the child on the first strip.

G1-315.title: Missing Ordinal Numbers Worksheet for 1st Grade | Free Printable PDF
G1-315.metaDescription: Write the missing ordinal numbers: three lines of eight zoo animals from a flag, four places printed — 1st, 3rd, 4th, 6th — four boxes to fill. Free 1st grade PDF.
G1-315.p1: Eight zoo animals stand in each of the three lines on this 1st grade page, behind a flag and an arrow, and under every animal is a box. Four of the eight boxes in each line are already written and four are empty: the first line shows 1st, 3rd, 4th and 6th and leaves 2nd, 5th, 7th and 8th blank; the third shows 1st, 2nd, 4th and 8th. The child counts from the flag and writes the missing ordinal number in each empty box — the numeral and its ending, 2nd, 5th, 7th, 8th. Twelve boxes to fill across the page, and 1st is given on every line.
G1-315.p2: Writing the notation is the new skill here. On the Kindergarten pages the child only marks a place; now they have to produce 2nd, 3rd and the -th endings, and the printed boxes are the model — a child who is unsure how to write 7th can look along the line to 6th and 8th. Because the gaps fall in different places on each line, the child cannot copy a pattern from the strip above; each box has to be counted from its own flag. A line of eight reaches the -th endings that only begin at 4th, which is where the spelling work is.
G1-315.p3: One sheet, pencil, twelve short answers. This is the writing face of the ordinal-numbers family, a step above the find-the-place base page; the ordinal-words page swaps the numerals for the words second to eighth, and the which-place page asks for the number from a picture instead of a box. The animals are the wave's zoo theme.

G1-316.h1: Ordinal Words: Draw a Line to the Picture
G1-316.title: Ordinal Words Worksheet for 1st Grade – Farm Animals | Free Printable PDF
G1-316.metaDescription: Ordinal words: two lines of eight farm animals from a flag, five shuffled word chips under each — second, seventh, eighth; draw a line to that place. Free 1st grade PDF.
G1-316.p1: Two long strips fill this 1st grade page. In each, eight farm animals stand in a line behind a flag and an arrow — an ox, a rooster, a turkey, a foal, a goat, a cow and others on the sheet shown — and under the line, after a tall gap, sit five word chips in a shuffled row: second, third, seventh, fifth, eighth on the first strip; fifth, third, second, seventh, sixth on the second. The child reads each ordinal word, counts from the flag to that place, and draws a line up from the chip to the animal standing there. Five lines per strip, ten in all, and nothing to write.
G1-316.p2: The ordinal stands alone as a word here — no numeral, no sentence around it — so the child has to read seventh and know it means the seventh place, which is the reading half of ordinal numbers. The chips are shuffled and the gap between them and the animals is deliberately tall: the lines have to cross, and a child who draws them in order finds the page tidier than one who does not. Only five of the eight places are asked for on each strip, so three animals get no line and the child cannot finish by elimination.
G1-316.p3: It prints on one sheet; a ruler keeps the ten lines legible. This is the word-reading face of the ordinal-numbers family — the write-the-missing page produces the numerals, this page reads the words. The farm theme is the wave's; the base find-the-place page uses animals at large and a numeral on the chip instead of a word.

G1-317.h1: Which Place? Write the Ordinal Number
G1-317.title: Which Place Ordinal Numbers Worksheet for 1st Grade | Free Printable PDF
G1-317.metaDescription: Which place: three lines of eight pets from a flag; two small pictures under each line with a box — find the pet and write its place, 2nd, 5th, 7th. Free 1st grade PDF.
G1-317.p1: Three lines of eight pets stand behind flags on this 1st grade page — a frog, a canary, a hamster, a tortoise, a puppy, a gecko, a chinchilla and a lizard in the first line on the sheet shown. Under each line sit two queries: a small copy of one of the pets, an arrow, and an empty dashed box. The child finds that pet in the line above, counts from the flag to it, and writes its place in the box as an ordinal number — the canary is 2nd, the puppy 5th. Six boxes across the page, each one counted from its own flag.
G1-317.p2: This is the ordinal in the other direction. The base page gives the number and asks for the picture; the write-the-missing page gives the line with gaps; here the picture is given and the number has to be produced from scratch, so nothing on the page shows the child what to write. Each line holds eight distinct pets so the small picture matches exactly one, and the two queries per line are always different animals in different places. A child who writes 5 instead of 5th has counted correctly and missed the ending, which is what the box is there to catch.
G1-317.p3: One sheet, six short answers. This is the most demanding of the three 1st grade faces in the ordinal-numbers family, because nothing is printed to copy; use it after the write-the-missing page, where four ordinals are given as models. The pets are the wave's theme; the family's base and either-end pages sit at Kindergarten with a mark instead of a written answer.

K-336.h1: Ordinal Numbers from Either End: Start at the Flag
K-336.title: Ordinals from Either End Worksheet for Kindergarten | Free Printable PDF
K-336.metaDescription: Ordinal numbers from either end: three lines of seven vehicles; the flag stands at the left or the right — find it, count from it, mark the place. Free Kindergarten PDF.
K-336.p1: Seven vehicles stand in each of the three lines on this Kindergarten page — a submarine, an ambulance, a forklift, a train and more on the sheet shown — under an arrow with a flag at one end. On two lines the flag is at the left and the arrow runs right; on the third the flag is at the right and the arrow runs left. Two chips under each line give a place and a mark — 5th with a circle, 7th with a cross; 3rd with a circle, 6th with a cross — and the child must find the flag first, count from that end, and make the mark on the vehicle in that place.
K-336.p2: Everything on this page is the base find-the-place page except the one thing that matters: the starting end is no longer fixed. That is the real definition of an ordinal — 3rd from where — and a child who counts from the left out of habit will mark the wrong vehicle on the reversed line. The page always carries at least one line in each direction, so the habit is tested every time. The teacher's prompt is the title itself: where is the flag? Say it before the child counts, on every strip.
K-336.p3: It prints on one sheet, pencil only. This is the either-end face of the ordinal-numbers family and the natural second page after the base, at the same Kindergarten level and with the same circle-and-cross chips. The vehicles are the wave's theme. When the reversed line is secure, the 1st grade pages move on to writing and reading the ordinal itself.

G1-318.h1: Who Wins the Race? Write the Place
G1-318.title: Who Wins the Race Worksheet for 1st Grade | Free Printable PDF
G1-318.metaDescription: Who wins the race: six lanes, one animal racer in each at its own distance from the finish line; the nearest is 1st — write 1st to 6th in the boxes. Free 1st grade PDF.
G1-318.p1: Six lanes stack down this 1st grade page, each a long card with a dashed track running from the left, a chequered finish line at the right, and an empty box beyond it.
