One animal racer sits in each lane, and every racer is a different distance from the finish — on the sheet shown a camel is almost touching the line, a horse and a tiger are behind it, a fish is near the middle, and a rabbit and a hippo have barely left the start. The child looks at how far each racer has to go, decides who is nearest, and writes 1st in that box, then 2nd, 3rd and on to 6th.
G1-318.p2: No two racers are level, so there is exactly one order, but it has to be read off distance rather than counted along a line, which is what makes this page different from every other ordinal page in the family. There is no flag: the finish line is the reference and nearest means first. Children who read the lanes top to bottom and write 1st at the top have answered a question the page did not ask; the racer in the fourth lane down is the winner here. The six animals come from the wave's animals theme.
G1-318.p3: One sheet, six boxes. This is the race face of the ordinal-numbers family, the page where the ordinals come from a comparison instead of a count from a flag, and the only one with a finish line. It works well read aloud as a commentary — the camel is in first place, the horse is second. The write-the-missing-ordinal-numbers page is the notation practice to pair with it.

K-321.h1: Days of the Week in Order
K-321.title: Days of the Week in Order for Kindergarten | Free Printable PDF
K-321.metaDescription: Days of the week worksheet: seven day names in a scrambled column, Sunday already marked 1. Number the rest 2 to 7 in the order they come. Free Kindergarten PDF.
K-321.p1: This kindergarten days-of-the-week worksheet prints the seven day names in one tall column, scrambled: Wednesday at the top, then Tuesday, Friday, Thursday, Saturday, Monday, and Sunday at the bottom. Beside each name sits a dashed square, and the square next to Sunday is already filled with a 1, shaded teal so it stands out. The child reads each name, works out where it falls in the week, and writes 2 to 7 in the empty squares. Nothing else is on the page: no pictures, no word bank, no writing lines, just names and numbers.
K-321.p2: Ordering by writing a rank number, rather than copying names, is the right first step for a child who can recognize the day names but cannot yet spell them. The given 1 fixes the start of the week (Sunday, as on an American calendar) so every other answer follows from it, and because the column is scrambled the child cannot just count down the page. The teacher watches what happens after Saturday: a child who reaches 7 and then looks for the day after Saturday has understood that the week is a cycle, not a list.
K-321.p3: It prints on one sheet in portrait, no color needed. Use it after the morning calendar routine, when the names are fresh, and let the child say the week aloud once with a finger on each number. The missing days page is the natural next step, where the child writes the names into gaps on a ladder, and the months of the year in order page repeats this exact numbering act on the twelve-month cycle. Reading a month grid and answering date questions is the calendar family at grade 2.

K-337.h1: Missing Days: Write the Week in Order
K-337.title: Missing Days of the Week Worksheet for Kindergarten | Free Printable PDF
K-337.metaDescription: Missing days worksheet: a week ladder with Sunday, Tuesday, Wednesday and Friday printed, three blank rungs and a word bank of all seven names. Free Kindergarten PDF.
K-337.p1: A word bank runs across the top of this kindergarten page, with all seven day names in pill shapes in a scrambled order. Below it an orange arrow runs down the left edge past a ladder of seven rungs. Four rungs carry a printed name, Sunday, Tuesday, Wednesday and Friday, and three are dashed boxes with a three-line handwriting guide inside. The child finds which days are missing, picks each one out of the bank, and copies it onto the rung where it belongs. The gaps are never side by side, so every blank has a printed name next to it to count from.
K-337.p2: This face asks for something the base page does not: writing the names. Because the bank carries every day, not only the missing three, the child first has to decide which names are already on the ladder, which is a matching-and-checking task in its own right, and only then copy. The printed neighbors above and below each gap give the child two anchors, so the day can be reasoned out (after Sunday, before Tuesday) rather than recalled cold. The teacher looks at the copying: whether the capital letter and the -day ending arrive intact.
K-337.p3: The handwriting guides are kindergarten-sized, with a dashed midline. Print it after the days of the week in order page, once the sequence itself is secure, and before yesterday, today, tomorrow, which asks the child to write neighbors with no bank at all. Keep the bank covered for a confident writer and reveal it only for spelling checks. The abbreviations page is the other writing-light option in this family.

G1-319.title: Yesterday, Today, Tomorrow Worksheet for 1st Grade | Free Printable PDF
G1-319.metaDescription: Yesterday, today, tomorrow worksheet: six rows, one day printed in the middle of each, blank boxes on both sides for the day before and the day after. Free 1st grade PDF.
G1-319.p1: Six rows, each with a day name printed in the middle and two dashed writing boxes either side, make up this first-grade page from the days-and-months set. Three headings across the top, yesterday, today, tomorrow, tell the child what each column means, and small orange arrows point left and right out of the middle box. The given days are scrambled: Wednesday, Monday, Sunday, Tuesday, Friday, Thursday. For each row the child writes the day that came before on the left and the day that comes next on the right, twelve names in all, with no word bank to copy from.
G1-319.p2: The move from ordering the week to naming a day's neighbors is the move from a list to a cycle, and the rows that include Sunday and Saturday are where it shows. Yesterday for Sunday is Saturday, and tomorrow for Saturday is Sunday, which a child who pictures the week as a straight line cannot answer. The page deliberately puts Sunday in the middle of a row so that the wrap has to happen at least once. Spelling twelve day names from memory is the second demand, and the teacher should decide in advance whether spelling counts.
G1-319.p3: It prints as a single portrait sheet with three-line guides in every box. A calendar on the wall, or the missing days page done first, gives a child who stalls a place to look. The month before and after page uses the same three-column layout on the twelve months, and the abbreviations page returns to the days with a much lighter writing load. This is the last of the three day pages in the family; the seasons pages take the year from here.

G1-320.h1: Months of the Year in Order
G1-320.title: Months of the Year in Order Worksheet for 1st Grade | Free Printable PDF
G1-320.metaDescription: Months of the year worksheet: twelve month names scrambled in two columns, January already marked 1, dashed boxes to number the others 2 to 12. Free 1st grade PDF.
G1-320.p1: Twelve month names, scrambled and laid out in two columns of six, fill this first-grade page: September, August, January, May, July, April, June, March, October, February, December, November. Each name has a dashed square to its left, and the square beside January already holds a 1 in a shaded box. The child numbers the other eleven months 2 to 12 in calendar order. It is the same numbering act as the days-and-months base page, moved from a seven-name cycle to a twelve-name one, with the extra demand that the numbers now run into two digits.
G1-320.p2: Month order is learned later and more slowly than day order, because months are rarely said as a chant in the classroom and the names carry no built-in clue. Numbering rather than writing keeps the load on sequence alone: the child does not have to spell February to place it. The two-column layout also means the eye cannot drift down one column, so each month must be located from memory. The teacher listens for the strategy: many children say the months quietly from January and count on their fingers, which is exactly the strategy the page rewards.
G1-320.p3: One sheet, portrait, no color required. It sits well next to a classroom calendar and works as a quick warm-up at the turn of any month. The month before and after page follows directly, asking the child to write a month's two neighbors, and the months and seasons page groups the same twelve names by season. The days of the week in order page is the kindergarten version of this act.

G1-321.title: The Month Before and After Worksheet for 1st Grade | Free Printable PDF
G1-321.metaDescription: Month before and after worksheet: six rows with one month printed in the middle, blank boxes on each side for the month before and the month after. Free 1st grade PDF.
G1-321.p1: The headings before and after sit at the top of this first-grade page, and under them run six rows from the days-and-months family. In the middle of each row one month is printed: August, July, December, March, June, February. On both sides is a dashed box with a three-line writing guide, and orange arrows point away from the printed name. The child writes the month that comes before on the left and the month that comes after on the right, twelve month names in total, with no bank to copy from and no calendar on the page.
G1-321.p2: Naming a month's neighbors is harder than numbering the months, because the child has to enter the cycle at an arbitrary point and move one step in each direction. The row with December is the one that matters most: the month after December is January, and a child who cannot answer that still thinks of the year as a line with an end. Spelling is the second load, and February and August are long words for this age, so a teacher may accept a good phonetic attempt and correct it afterwards rather than treat it as wrong.
G1-321.p3: It prints on one portrait sheet. Have the child say the months aloud from January before starting, and keep the months of the year in order page nearby as a reference the first time. The yesterday, today, tomorrow page is the identical layout on the days of the week, and the months and seasons page follows with a coloring task on the same twelve names. Month grids and date questions belong to the calendar family at grade 2.

G1-322.title: Days of the Week Abbreviations Worksheet for 1st Grade | Free Printable PDF
G1-322.metaDescription: Days of the week abbreviations worksheet: Sun, Mon, Tue, Wed, Thu, Fri and Sat in one column, the seven full names scrambled in another, match them. Free 1st grade PDF.
G1-322.p1: Seven short forms run down the left of this first-grade days-and-months page in week order, Sun, Mon, Tue, Wed, Thu, Fri, Sat, each in a white box with an orange dot beside it. Down the right side the full day names sit in cream boxes, scrambled so that no short form lines up with its own name: Wednesday, Friday, Saturday, Thursday, Monday, Sunday, Tuesday. The child reads a short form, finds the day it stands for, and draws a line from dot to dot. Seven lines finish the page; nothing is written.
G1-322.p2: Three-letter day abbreviations are everywhere a child looks, on the classroom calendar, a phone, a bus timetable, and this page makes them a reading task rather than something to absorb by accident. Because the short forms are in week order, the child can also use the sequence as a check: if Thu has been matched to Tuesday, the lines will cross where they should not. The teacher watches Tue and Thu, the pair that shares a first letter, and Sat and Sun, which share two.
G1-322.p3: A one-sheet print with no color needed and no writing lines, so it suits a child whose handwriting is still slow. Use it once the days of the week in order page is easy, and pair it with a look at the real calendar to find the same short forms. The yesterday, today, tomorrow page and the missing days page are the writing-heavy siblings in this family.

K-322.title: Four Seasons Sort Worksheet for Kindergarten | Free Printable PDF
K-322.metaDescription: Four seasons worksheet: eight pictures and four season boxes with a snowflake, flower, sun and leaf sign — draw a line from each picture to its season. Free K PDF.
K-322.p1: Eight pictures and four season boxes make up this kindergarten seasons page. A row of four pictures runs across the top, a row of four across the bottom, and in between sit the boxes, each with its sign and its name: a snowflake for Winter, a flower for Spring, a sun for Summer, a leaf for Fall. The pictures in this print are an ice skater, a seashell, a tulip bud, a sled, a red-leaved tree, a chick, a basket of apples and a swimmer. Every picture has an orange dot, every box has a dot on its top and bottom edge, and the child draws a line from picture to box. Two pictures belong to each season.
K-322.p2: Sorting is the first thing a child can do with the seasons, before ordering them and long before naming their months. The page keeps the reasoning visible: a line is a decision the teacher can see and talk about, and a sled going to Summer is a conversation, not a mark. The signs matter as much as the names, because the other pages in this family use the same four signs without the words. The teacher listens for the reason behind each line; the chick belongs to Spring because that is when chicks hatch, not because it is yellow.
K-322.p3: It prints in color, since the pictures carry the information, on one portrait sheet. Do it as a group first with the pictures named aloud, then individually. The which season is it page is the next step, with three pictures per card and the sign to circle; what does not belong flips the task into finding the intruder. Clothes for hot and cold weather, and the month names in order, are their own worksheet types.

K-338.title: Which Season Is It? Worksheet for Kindergarten | Free Printable PDF
K-338.metaDescription: Which season is it worksheet: four cards, three pictures on each from one season, four season signs below — circle the sign the pictures belong to. Free K PDF.
K-338.p1: Four numbered cards fill this kindergarten seasons page, two across and two down. Each card shows three pictures that all come from one season, and under them a row of four small season signs: snowflake, flower, sun, leaf. On this print card 1 has a tent, a watermelon slice and a beach, card 2 a snowman, an ice skater and a skier, card 3 a tulip bud, a tulip and a nest of chicks, card 4 an acorn, a pumpkin and a basket of apples. The child looks at the three pictures together, decides which season they share, and circles that sign. Each card is a different season, so all four signs get used once.
K-338.p2: Where the base page sorts one picture at a time, this face asks the child to read three at once and find what they have in common, which is a step up in reasoning. One picture on its own can be argued (a basket of apples could be Summer), but three together settle it, and the child learns to look for agreement. The signs carry no name, so the page also checks that the snowflake, flower, sun and leaf are now attached to the seasons in the child's mind and not just to the word beside them.
K-338.p3: A one-sheet color print. Cover the answer row with a finger and have the child say the season before circling, then compare. The four seasons sort page is the warm-up if the signs are still unfamiliar, the seasons what does not belong page is the mirror task where three agree and one intrudes, and the season wheel turns to the order of the seasons.

K-339.title: Season Wheel: Seasons in Order for Kindergarten | Free Printable PDF
K-339.metaDescription: Season wheel worksheet: four slots joined by arrows, Winter already drawn in, three empty circles and a bank of the missing signs to draw in order. Free K PDF.
K-339.p1: One large wheel sits in the middle of this kindergarten seasons page: four circles arranged like the points of a compass, joined by orange arrows that run clockwise. The top circle is filled in with a snowflake and the word Winter. The other three are dashed and empty. Below the wheel a bank shows the three missing signs with their names, Fall, Spring and Summer, in a scrambled order. The child works out which season follows Winter, draws its sign in the next circle along the arrow, and carries on round until the wheel is complete. Nothing is written, only drawn.
K-339.p2: The wheel is the first place a child meets the idea that the seasons come back around, which a list on a wall never shows. Because only one season is given and the arrows fix the direction, there is exactly one correct filling, and the child has to reason from the neighbor rather than from a memorized chant. Drawing the sign instead of writing the word keeps the task within reach at this age, and the bank removes the need to invent a symbol. The teacher watches whether the child follows the arrows or fills the circles in reading order.
K-339.p3: It prints on one portrait sheet and works in black and white, since the signs are line drawings. A child who finishes can be asked to say the wheel aloud starting from any circle. The four seasons sort page and which season is it page come before this one; the months and seasons page at first grade puts the twelve months onto the same four-season order, and the draw the tree page shows the cycle through one tree.

K-340.title: Seasons: What Does Not Belong? for Kindergarten | Free Printable PDF
K-340.metaDescription: Seasons what does not belong worksheet: four rows of four pictures, three from one season and one from another, cross out the odd one in each row. Free Kindergarten PDF.
K-340.p1: Sixteen pictures in four numbered rows run down this kindergarten seasons page. In each row three pictures come from one season and one comes from somewhere else, and the child crosses out the one that does not belong. On this print the first row shows a snowboarder, an ice skater, a child on a sled and a swimming pool; the second an autumn tree, a bundle of wheat, a basket of apples and a pair of flip-flops; the third a tulip, a skier, a tulip bud and a duckling; the fourth a tent, a surfboard, a lamb and a swimmer. No words appear on the page, and no season signs, so the child works from the pictures alone.
K-340.p2: Finding the intruder is the reverse of the which season is it face: there the child looks for what three pictures share, here for the one that breaks the pattern. It is a classification task first and a seasons task second, and it can be done by a child who has not yet named a single season, which makes it a good first look at how much a child already knows. The teacher asks for the reason behind each cross. A child who crosses out the lamb because it is an animal, not because it belongs to Spring, has sorted by the wrong rule.
K-340.p3: One color sheet in portrait. Let the child name the pictures aloud before crossing anything out, since a mislabeled picture produces a confident wrong answer. The four seasons sort page is the gentler introduction with the signs and names printed, the which season is it page is the same rows turned around, and the season wheel moves on to order.

G1-323.h1: Months and Seasons: Color the Season
G1-323.title: Months and Seasons Worksheet for 1st Grade | Free Printable PDF
G1-323.metaDescription: Months and seasons worksheet: the twelve months in calendar order with a circle beside each and a color key, blue for winter through orange for fall. Free 1st grade PDF.
G1-323.p1: A color key across the top of this first-grade seasons page gives the four seasons with their signs and a swatch each: Winter blue, Spring green, Summer yellow, Fall orange. Below it twelve month cards run in calendar order, January to December in three columns of four, each with an empty circle to its right. The child reads each month, decides which season it falls in, and colors its circle in that season's color. Nothing is scrambled and nothing is written; the whole task is twelve reading-and-coloring decisions.
G1-323.p2: This is where the months and the seasons meet for the first time in the catalog. The months are in order because the point is the grouping, not the sequence: a child colors December, January and February blue and sees that a season is three months long and that winter straddles the turn of the year. The key does the naming, so the page can be done by a child who knows the seasons well but is still shaky on which month is which. The teacher looks at March and September, the months that start a season, where children most often color one month too early or too late.
G1-323.p3: It needs the four colors from the key, in crayon or pencil, on one portrait sheet. The months of the year in order page is the natural warm-up if the sequence is not yet secure, and the season wheel at kindergarten gives the four-season cycle the months are now attached to. A finished page makes a small season chart for the child's desk.

K-341.h1: Draw the Tree in Four Seasons
K-341.title: Draw the Tree in Four Seasons for Kindergarten | Free Printable PDF
K-341.metaDescription: Draw the tree in four seasons: four panels, Winter, Spring, Summer and Fall, the same bare tree in each to finish with snow, blossom or leaves. Free Kindergarten PDF.
K-341.p1: The same bare tree is printed four times on this kindergarten seasons page, once in each of four large panels labeled Winter, Spring, Summer and Fall, with the season's sign beside each label. The tree is a trunk and a fan of empty branches, drawn in outline, standing on a ground line. The child draws what the tree looks like in that season: bare branches and snow, buds and blossom, a full green crown, orange leaves in the air and on the ground. There is no right answer printed anywhere, only four empty trees.
K-341.p2: Every other page in this family asks the child to recognize a season; this one asks the child to produce it, which is a different and harder kind of knowing. Drawing the same tree four times makes the change itself the subject: the trunk never moves, only what grows on it. It is an open-ended page, so the teacher reads the drawings for what the child knows (blossom before leaves, leaves before bare) rather than marking them, and it makes a good talking page for a child who has more to say than to write.
K-341.p3: It prints on one portrait sheet and asks for colored pencils or crayons. Do it after a walk to look at a real tree, or spread across the year with one panel finished each season and the sheet kept in a folder. The four seasons sort page and the which season is it page are the recognition tasks that lead here, and the season wheel gives the order the four panels follow.

K-323.title: All About Me Worksheet for Kindergarten | Free Printable PDF
K-323.metaDescription: All about me worksheet: a name line, an age box, a frame to draw yourself, a family box, and three windows for a favorite animal, food and color. Free Kindergarten PDF.
K-323.p1: A name line, an age box, a self-portrait frame, a family box and three favorite-things windows: that is the whole of this kindergarten all-about-me page. The top band reads My name is beside a three-line handwriting guide. Below it a large dashed frame with photo corners is captioned This is me, and to its right sit a lane reading I am, a dashed square, years old, and a dashed box labeled My family. Across the bottom three tall windows are headed My favorite animal, My favorite food and My favorite color. The child writes a name and a numeral and draws everything else.
K-323.p2: An all-about-me page is usually the first piece of work a kindergartner produces, and it is designed so that every child can finish it: two things to write, five things to draw, no reading beyond the headings. It asks the child to record facts about himself or herself, which is the earliest form of informative writing, and the drawings are the child's answers. For the teacher it is a record of the first week: how the name is written, whether the age numeral is formed correctly, how many people appear in the family box. The same page done again in spring shows the year's growth.
K-323.p3: One portrait sheet, best printed on heavier paper if it is going on a wall or into a portfolio. The five faces of this family take one element each further: my favorite things adds pictures and words to choose from, all about my family adds ten-frames to the family box, label the face, I can, and my name each take one corner of this page and make it a lesson. No feelings, no animal fact file, no story starter: this page is about the child.

K-342.h1: My Favorite Things: Circle and Write
K-342.title: My Favorite Things Worksheet for Kindergarten | Free Printable PDF
K-342.metaDescription: My favorite things worksheet: three rows of six labeled pictures — animals, foods, colors — circle a favorite in each row and copy its word. Free Kindergarten PDF.
K-342.p1: Three rows, each headed My favorite animal, My favorite food or My favorite color, give this kindergarten page its shape. Every row holds six picture tiles with the word printed under each: on this print fish, duck, pig, giraffe, tiger and sheep; cake, grapes, milk, pizza, carrot and cookie; and six color squares, orange, yellow, purple, blue, green and red. Under each row an arrow points to a three-line handwriting guide. The child circles one tile per row and copies its word onto the line. Three circles and three words finish the page.
K-342.p2: On the base all-about-me page the favorites are drawn; here they are chosen from a set and written, which turns a drawing task into a reading-and-copying one. The choice is real, so the word the child copies is a word the child wanted to say, and that is the best condition for careful copying there is. Every printed word is a model, so spelling is not being tested, only letter formation and word spacing. The teacher looks at the copy against the tile: which letters were dropped, and whether the word was written as one piece.
K-342.p3: A one-page color print, since the pictures do the naming. Read the six words of each row aloud with the child first so the choice is made from all six and not just the pictures the child can name alone. The all about me page is the drawing version of the same three favorites, and the my name page is the other copying task in this family. Sorting or matching pictures to words is a different worksheet type.

K-343.h1: All About My Family: Draw and Count
K-343.title: All About My Family Worksheet for Kindergarten | Free Printable PDF
K-343.metaDescription: All about my family worksheet: a big box to draw the family, then four ten-frames for people, brothers, sisters and pets, each with a number box. Free Kindergarten PDF.
K-343.p1: The top third of this kindergarten page is one wide dashed box labeled Draw your family. Under it are four numbered cards: People in my family, Brothers, Sisters and Pets. Each card holds an empty ten-frame, two rows of five cells, and a dashed square in its corner for a numeral. The child draws the family first, then fills one cell of the ten-frame for each person, brother, sister or pet, and writes how many in the square. A child with no pets leaves that frame empty and writes 0, which is a real answer on this page.
K-343.p2: The counting here is of something the child knows better than anything else, and that is the point: the number is not read off printed dots but produced from memory, then shown on the frame and written as a numeral, three representations of one quantity. The four categories overlap, since brothers and sisters are also people, and a child who notices that has understood something about sets. Zero is allowed and expected for at least one card in most families, which makes this one of the few pages where a kindergartner writes 0 for a reason. The teacher compares the drawing with the People frame: they should agree.
K-343.p3: A one-sheet portrait print that works in black and white. Do it as a talking page, with the child naming everyone in the drawing before counting. The all about me base page has a smaller family box with no counting, and the my name page is the family's other counting face, where the child counts letters instead of people. Printed dots to count are the counting-frames family, not this one.

K-344.h1: This Is Me: Label the Face
K-344.title: Label the Face Worksheet for Kindergarten | Free Printable PDF
K-344.metaDescription: Label the face worksheet: a child's face with five pointer lines, a word bank of mouth, hair, nose, eye and ear to copy, then a box to draw your own face. Free K PDF.
K-344.p1: Five words sit in a dashed bank at the top of this kindergarten page: mouth, hair, nose, eye, ear. Below it a large illustrated face of a child looks out from the middle of the sheet, with five orange dots on the hair, one eye, the nose, one ear and the mouth, and a line from each dot to a dashed handwriting box at the edge of the page. The child reads a word, finds the part it names, and copies the word into the box its line leads to. At the bottom a wide dashed box reads Now draw your own face.
K-344.p2: Labeling a diagram is a skill in its own right, separate from knowing the words: the child has to follow a line from a dot to a box and put the word there, not next to the part itself. Because the five words are given, the reading load is light and the task is really about matching and copying. The drawn face is deliberately neutral, a small smile and nothing more, so that no feeling is being read. The teacher checks the eye and nose boxes, the two whose lines cross the face and can be mistaken for each other.
K-344.p3: One portrait sheet, color helpful but not needed. The draw-your-own box at the bottom is the reward, and the labels can be reused on the child's own drawing. The all about me page has the self-portrait without labels, and the my name page is the family's other copying task. Reading a feeling off a face is the emotions worksheet family, not this page.

K-345.h1: I Can: Tick What You Can Do
K-345.title: I Can: Tick What You Can Do for Kindergarten | Free Printable PDF
K-345.metaDescription: I can worksheet: eight picture cards, each with a sentence such as I can ride a bike and a box to tick, then a line to finish I want to learn to. Free Kindergarten PDF.
K-345.p1: Eight cards in two columns, each with a dashed tick box, a picture and a short sentence, make up this kindergarten page: I can paint a picture, I can brush my teeth, I can sing a song, I can ride a bike, I can run, I can swim, I can read a book, I can kick a ball. The pictures show the object or the action, a paintbrush and palette, a toothbrush, a microphone, a child on a bike. Under the cards a wide lane begins I want to learn to, with a three-line handwriting guide. The child reads each sentence, ticks the ones that are true, and writes one thing to learn.
K-345.p2: The same two words open every sentence, so after the first card the child is reading I can by sight and only the last two or three words change, which is how a sentence frame teaches. There is no wrong tick, because only the child knows the answer, and that is what makes it an all-about-me page rather than a reading test. The writing at the bottom is the one open line: a real wish, spelled however the child can spell it. The teacher reads the ticks as a portrait and the last line as the child's first sentence of the year.
K-345.p3: A one-sheet portrait print, color for the pictures. Read the eight sentences aloud together before the child works alone, and keep the finished page, since the empty boxes are the ones to tick in June. The all about me page is the drawing version of the same self-report, and my favorite things is the other choosing page. Story starters and picture writing are a separate worksheet family.

K-346.h1: My Name: Write, Count and Compare
K-346.title: My Name: Write, Count and Compare for Kindergarten | Free Printable PDF
K-346.metaDescription: My name worksheet: write your name on a line and again one letter per box, count the letters, then do the same for a friend and circle who has more. Free K PDF.
K-346.p1: This kindergarten page is built in two matching halves. The top half reads My name over a handwriting line, then a strip of ten dashed letter boxes with the note Write one letter in each box, then two small cards: Letters in my name, with a square for the count, and The first letter of my name, with a square for the letter. The bottom half repeats the line and the ten boxes for My friend's name. At the foot a band asks Who has more letters? with two ovals to circle, me and my friend. The child writes, counts, and compares.
K-346.p2: A child's own name is the first word most children can write, and putting it one letter per box turns it into something that can be counted, which is the first time many children see that a word is made of a fixed number of pieces. Writing the first letter on its own draws attention to the capital. The comparison with a friend's name is the mathematics: two counts, and a decision about which is larger, made on numbers the child produced. The teacher watches whether the count matches the boxes filled and whether the child compares by counting or by looking at the row lengths.
K-346.p3: It prints on one portrait sheet in black and white. Pair children up so the friend's name is copied from a name card, not spelled from memory. If both names are the same length there is no oval for a tie, so tell the child to circle both. The all about me page has the name line alone, and all about my family is the sibling counting page with ten-frames instead of letter boxes.

K-324.title: Picture Word Cards for Kindergarten – Animals | Free Printable PDF
K-324.metaDescription: Picture word cards to cut out: eight animal cards on one sheet, a picture with its word printed under it, for naming, reading and a classroom word wall. Free K PDF.
K-324.p1: Eight cut-out cards on one sheet, two across and four down, make up this kindergarten set of animals picture word cards. Each card shows one animal drawn large with its word in a cream label underneath: on this print penguin, antelope, seagull, moose, cat, camel, wolf and bat. Dotted lines with a scissors mark run between the cards. The child cuts the sheet into eight, then takes each card, says the name of the picture, and reads the word under it. Nothing is written on the page and nothing is drawn.
K-324.p2: A picture word card is the simplest reading object there is: the picture tells the child what the word says, so the child can read a word like antelope long before sounding it out is possible, and each success is real. The cards outlive the sheet. They go on a word wall, into a pocket chart, or into a bag for a five-minute naming game, and the same eight animals are met again and again until the words are known on sight. The teacher listens to the naming: a child who says bird for seagull has read the picture but not yet the word.
K-324.p3: Print in color on card stock if the set is going to be handled, and cut with the child if scissors are part of the lesson. The five faces of this family change one thing each: the matching pairs set splits picture and word onto separate cards, the a or an cards add the article, one and many prints singular beside plural, the bilingual cards add Spanish, and the syllable cards break each word into parts. These are cut-out cards with nothing to write; matching pictures to words on a page is a different worksheet type.

K-347.h1: Picture Cards and Word Cards: Matching Pairs
K-347.title: Picture and Word Cards Matching Pairs – Fruits | Free Printable PDF
K-347.metaDescription: Picture and word cards to cut out and match: eight fruit picture cards and eight separate word cards on one sheet, for pairing or a game of Memory. Free Kindergarten PDF.
K-347.p1: Sixteen cards in a four-by-four grid fill this kindergarten sheet of fruits cards. The top two rows are picture cards with no words: on this print a blueberry, a nectarine, a banana, a papaya, a cranberry, a pomegranate, a pear and a raspberry. The bottom two rows are word cards with no pictures, and they are shuffled so no word sits under its own picture: banana, cranberry, nectarine, pomegranate, raspberry, pear, papaya, blueberry. The child cuts out all sixteen, then lays each word card beside the picture it names, or turns the lot face down and plays Memory, lifting two at a time to find a pair.
K-347.p2: Separating the word from its picture is the difference between this set and the base cards. On a single card the picture reads the word for the child; here the child has to read the word alone, at least far enough to tell banana from blueberry by the first letters, and then find its picture. Memory adds a second thing to hold in mind, where each card was, and it works as a two-player game with no losing that matters. The teacher watches the two b-words and the two p-words, where a child reading only the first letter will pair wrongly.
K-347.p3: A color print on card stock lasts longest; cut all sixteen before the lesson if time is short. The picture word cards base set is the naming version with word and picture on one card, and a or an cards, one and many, bilingual and syllable cards each change a different thing. Cut-out cards, nothing to write.

K-348.h1: A or An: Word Cards with the Article
K-348.title: A or An Word Cards with the Article – Vehicles | Free Printable PDF
K-348.metaDescription: A or an word cards to cut out: eight vehicle picture cards with the article printed before each word — a helicopter, an ambulance — to say aloud. Free Kindergarten PDF.
K-348.p1: Every word on this kindergarten sheet of vehicles is printed with its article in front of it, and there are eight cut-out cards, two by four: on this print a helicopter, a submarine, a bicycle, a skateboard, an ambulance, a sailboat, a jeep, a canoe. The article is part of the label, in the same lettering as the noun, so the card reads as a two-word phrase. The child cuts the cards apart and says each one exactly as it is written, article and all. There is nothing to choose and nothing to write; the page shows the right form and the child says it.
K-348.p2: Most a-or-an pages ask the child to pick the article, and get it wrong half the time. This set does the opposite: it shows the correct phrase and asks only that it be said, so the ear gets a helicopter and an ambulance as whole sounds before any rule is taught. The rule follows from the ear, not the other way around. Which words draw an depends on the eight the sheet happens to print, since it is one draw from the vehicles pool, and a set with only one an is still doing its job. The teacher listens for the article being said, not dropped.
K-348.p3: Color print, card stock for a class set, and keep the cards for a pocket chart where the article stays attached to its noun. The picture word cards base set is the same eight-card layout without the article, and the one and many cards move on to plural forms. Circling a or an as an answer is the a or an worksheet family, not this one.

K-349.h1: One and Many: Singular and Plural Cards
K-349.title: One and Many Singular and Plural Cards – Toys | Free Printable PDF
K-349.metaDescription: Singular and plural cards to cut out: four toy pairs, one picture with its word beside three of the same with the plural — train, trains; baby, babies. Free K PDF.
K-349.p1: Four pairs of cards, eight in all, make up this kindergarten sheet of toys. The left column shows one picture with its singular word, the right column shows three of the same picture with the plural: on this print train and trains, ball and balls, airplane and airplanes, baby and babies. The pictures are the same size on both cards, so the number of them is the only thing that changes. The child cuts out all eight, says the word for one and the word for many, and, once the cards are shuffled, matches each singular to its plural.
K-349.p2: Printing both forms, rather than asking the child to write the plural, keeps the attention on hearing and seeing the ending: trains is train with an s, and the three pictures say why. When the draw includes a word like baby, the child meets a plural that changes its spelling as well, which is worth a sentence from the teacher and no more at this age. Matching after shuffling is the check: a child who pairs ball with balls by reading the start of the word and counting the pictures has done what the card is for.
K-349.p3: Print in color on card stock and cut before the lesson for a class set. The picture word cards base set gives one picture per card with no plural, and the a or an cards attach the article instead of the ending. Writing the plural on a line is the singular and plural worksheet family, which is the next step after these cards.

K-350.h1: Bilingual Picture Cards: English and Spanish
K-350.title: Bilingual Picture Cards: English and Spanish | Free Printable PDF
K-350.metaDescription: Bilingual picture cards to cut out: eight zoo animal cards with the English word above the Spanish — bear and oso, lion and león — for a word wall. Free Kindergarten PDF.
K-350.p1: Two words sit under every picture on this kindergarten sheet of zoo animals: the English word in dark lettering and the Spanish word in teal beneath it. There are eight cut-out cards, and on this print the pairs are bear and oso, lion and león, jaguar and jaguar, kangaroo and canguro, rhinoceros and rinoceronte, orangutan and orangután, otter and nutria, koala and koala. A small legend above the cards reads English and Spanish. The child cuts the cards apart, says each word in English, then in Spanish, and keeps the set for the word wall.
K-350.p2: A two-language card does something a picture dictionary cannot: it puts both names on one object the child can hold, so the Spanish word is learned as another name for the same bear, not as a translation of an English word. The draw here is kind to a beginner, since several animals share a name or nearly share one across the two languages, and the accents in the Spanish forms are printed as a Spanish reader would expect them. In a dual-language or Spanish-immersion class the cards go up in both languages at once; in an English classroom they are a first Spanish set.
K-350.p3: Color print on card stock, and keep the pairs intact rather than cutting the two words apart. The picture word cards base set is the one-language version of the same layout, and the syllable cards at first grade break the English words into parts. Cut-out cards, nothing to write; crossword and word-search pages in a second language are a separate family.

G1-324.h1: Syllable Cards: Read the Word in Parts
G1-324.title: Syllable Cards for 1st Grade – Animals | Free Printable PDF
G1-324.metaDescription: Syllable cards to cut out: eight animal picture cards with the word spaced out letter by letter and an arc under each syllable — dol-phin, rab-bit. Free 1st grade PDF.
G1-324.p1: The word under each picture on this first-grade sheet of animals syllable cards is printed with its letters spaced apart, and beneath the letters a green arc spans each syllable: on this print dol-phin, rab-bit, vul-ture, rein-deer, don-key, pen-guin, pan-da and rac-coon. There are eight cut-out cards, two by four. The child cuts them apart, reads each word one arc at a time with a finger under the arc, then says the whole word. The split is printed, so the child never has to decide where a syllable ends.
G1-324.p2: A first-grade reader stalls on a long word not because the letters are hard but because the whole thing is too much to hold at once; the arcs cut it into pieces of two or three letters each, which is exactly the size a child can decode. The words on the sheet come from a pool of animal names of two to four syllables, checked against a standard hyphenation dictionary, so every arc sits where a dictionary would put it. Reading the parts and then the whole is the routine, and the teacher listens for the join, the moment the two chunks become one word.
G1-324.p3: A color print, card stock if the cards will be reused, and a finger or a coin to slide from arc to arc. The picture word cards base set at kindergarten shows the same kind of words whole, and the one and many cards move to plural endings. Drawing the syllable split yourself, or sorting words by syllable count, is the syllable worksheet family; these cards print the split for you.

G2-319.h1: Logic Grid Puzzles: Three Clues, One Answer
G2-319.title: Logic Grid Puzzles for 2nd Grade – Pets, Three Clues | Free Printable PDF
G2-319.metaDescription: Logic grid puzzles worksheet: two puzzles, three children and three pets each, three sentence clues, a grid to cross out and tick, an answer strip. Free 2nd grade PDF.
G2-319.p1: Two puzzles share this second-grade page, and each has the same parts: three numbered clues on the left, a three-by-three grid on the right with the children's names down the side and three pets across the top, and under it a strip of three answer boxes, one per child, each showing all three pictures. On this print the first puzzle has Ben, Mia and Tom with a mouse, a cat and a dog, and clues such as Tom does not have the mouse, with the animal drawn in place of its name. The child reads a clue, crosses out the cell it rules out, ticks a cell once it is the only one left in its row, and finally circles each child's pet in the strip.
G2-319.p2: This is the elimination puzzle in its simplest honest form: three negative clues, three children, one answer each, and every clue needed. A cross is a fact the child has established, a tick is a conclusion drawn from two crosses, and the grid makes the reasoning visible on paper so a wrong answer can be traced back to the clue that caused it. The pictures in the clues, in place of nouns, keep the reading load low for a second grader. The teacher watches for the tick that follows two crosses in a row, and for the cross that a tick forces in the rest of its column.
G2-319.p3: One portrait sheet, color helpful for the pictures. The legend of tick, cross and a filled row sits at the top right as a reminder. Work the first puzzle together and leave the second to the child. The five faces of this family each change one thing: the clue kinds, the grid size, picture clues instead of sentences, two attributes per child, or a grid already solved to read. Sudoku, with its rows and columns and no clues, is a different family.

G2-344.h1: Logic Grid Puzzles with Yes, No and Either-Or Clues
G2-344.title: Logic Grid Puzzles with Yes, No and Either-Or Clues | Free Printable PDF
G2-344.metaDescription: Logic grid puzzles with three clue types: a yes clue earns a tick, a no clue earns a cross, an either-or clue rules out the third fruit. Two puzzles. Free 2nd grade PDF.
G2-344.p1: The clues on this second-grade fruits page come in three kinds, and the instruction line names what each one does. Either a cherry or a strawberry belongs to Tom is an either-or clue: it crosses out the third fruit in Tom's row. The child with the strawberry is not Tom is a no clue: one cross. The pear belongs to Max is a yes clue: a tick, and crosses in the rest of that row and column. Two puzzles with three children each, one with three clues and one with two, share the page, and each has the answer strip underneath.
G2-344.p2: The base puzzles run on no clues alone; this face adds a clue that gives a fact outright and a clue that gives two possibilities, and the child has to know which mark each one earns before touching the grid. Either-or is the new idea. It does not say who has what, only what someone does not have, and turning or into a cross is a piece of reasoning most second graders have never been asked to write down. Every page carries at least one yes clue and at least one either-or, so both moves get practiced. The teacher checks that a tick brought its four crosses with it.
G2-344.p3: A one-sheet color print with the mark legend in the corner. Say each clue's kind aloud before marking, yes, no, or either-or, until the child does it unprompted. The three clues, one answer page is the base with no clues only; the true or false page reads a solved grid, and the picture clue page at first grade takes the sentences away.

G3-378.h1: 4 by 4 Logic Grid Puzzles: Six Clues
G3-378.title: 4 by 4 Logic Grid Puzzles for 3rd Grade – Six Clues | Free Printable PDF
G3-378.metaDescription: 4 by 4 logic grid puzzles: two puzzles with four children and four toys each, six clues, a sixteen-cell grid to cross out and tick, no answer strip. Free 3rd grade PDF.
G3-378.p1: Four children and four toys per puzzle, two puzzles to a page, six clues each: this third-grade face is the family's biggest grid. On this print the first puzzle gives Leo, Max, Mia and Ben with a train, a ball, a doll and a die, and the six clues are all things a child does not have, three of them about Mia. The grid has sixteen cells, and there is no answer strip below it; the four ticks the child writes into the grid are the answer. The mark legend sits at the top right as on the smaller puzzles.
G3-378.p2: Going from three to four is not one more row; it is a grid where a single clue eliminates less, so the child must combine clues before any row closes, and hold the state of sixteen cells rather than nine. Six clues is the number that makes the puzzle fair: with all six used, every row resolves, and a child who stops at four will find two rows still open. Three clues about one child is the deliberate pattern here, since three crosses in a row of four leave exactly one cell, the first tick, and everything else follows. The teacher looks for the order in which ticks were written.
G3-378.p3: One portrait sheet, color for the toys. Have the child number the crosses with the clue that caused them the first time, so a mistake can be found. The three clues, one answer page is the three-by-three base, the two-attribute page is the other third-grade face with two pictures per child, and the yes, no and either-or page brings in positive and either-or clues on the smaller grid.

G1-349.h1: Picture Clue Logic Puzzles: Cross Out and Find
G1-349.title: Picture Clue Logic Puzzles for 1st Grade – Vehicles | Free Printable PDF
G1-349.metaDescription: Picture clue logic puzzles: no sentences to read — each clue is a name tile and a vehicle picture, crossed out or ringed. Solve the grid. Free 1st grade PDF.
G1-349.p1: No clue on this first-grade vehicles page is a sentence. Each clue is a name in a box and, beside it, a picture inside a circle: a big orange cross over the picture means that child does not have it, a plain ring means the child does. On this print the first puzzle has Ben with a crossed-out plane and Mia with a ringed car, the second has Anna crossed out twice, for the submarine and the rocket, and Lily crossed out for the submarine. To the right sits a three-by-three grid with names and pictures, and below it the three answer strips to circle in.
G1-349.p2: A first grader can reason about who has what long before reading a sentence like the child with the boat is not Emma, and this face removes the reading so the reasoning shows on its own. The two pictograms are the whole vocabulary: cross means no, ring means yes, and they are the same marks the child makes on the grid. Every page shows both, so the yes move gets practiced as well as the elimination. Two or three clues is enough on a three-by-three grid, and a child who thinks a clue is missing has usually not yet used the row-and-column rule.
G1-349.p3: Print in color, since the vehicles have to be told apart at a glance, on one portrait sheet. Read the legend aloud, cross means does not have, ring means has, and then let the child go. The three clues, one answer page at second grade is the same grid with sentence clues, and the true or false page reads a finished grid. Picture sudoku is a different family: rows and columns, no children, no clues.

G3-379.h1: Two-Attribute Logic Puzzles: Two Pictures per Child
G3-379.title: Two-Attribute Logic Puzzles for 3rd Grade – Pets | Free Printable PDF
G3-379.metaDescription: Two-attribute logic puzzle: three children, each with one pet and one fruit, four clues including a linking clue, three joined grids in an L shape. Free 3rd grade PDF.
G3-379.p1: One puzzle fills this third-grade pets page, and it has three grids joined into an L. Across the top run three pets, a fish, a turtle and a rabbit, and then three fruits, a banana, an apple and a pear; down the side are Emma, Mia and Max, and below them the three fruits again. Every child has one pet and one fruit. Four clues sit above the grids, and one of them links the two sets: The child with the fish has the apple. The child fills all three grids, name to pet, name to fruit, and pet to fruit, and there is no answer strip; the ticks are the answer.
G3-379.p2: This is the real logic grid, the one found in puzzle books, cut down to three of everything. A linking clue is the new move: it says nothing about any child, only that two things go together, and the child has to carry that fact from the pet-fruit grid into the name grids once a name is pinned to one of them. The three grids must agree with each other at the end, which is a check the child can run alone. The teacher watches the third grid, the one with no names; it is where a child who has only ever done one-attribute puzzles stops marking.
G3-379.p3: One portrait sheet, color for the pictures. Have the child work the linking clue last the first time, then first the second time, and notice that both routes arrive at the same grid. The 4 by 4 page is the other third-grade face, with more children but one attribute, and the three clues, one answer page is the base this grows from.

G2-345.h1: Read the Logic Grid: True or False
G2-345.title: Read the Logic Grid True or False for 2nd Grade | Free Printable PDF
G2-345.metaDescription: Read the logic grid worksheet: two grids already solved with ticks and crosses, five sentences beside each — circle tick if true, cross if false. Free 2nd grade PDF.
G2-345.p1: Nothing on this grade-2 page has to be solved. Both grids come already filled in with ticks and crosses, three children and three zoo animals each, and the work is on the left: five numbered sentences per grid, each followed by a circled tick and a circled cross. On this print the first grid gives Tom the tiger, Ben the monkey and Mia the zebra, and the sentences read Ben does not have the zebra, Mia has the tiger, The child with the monkey is Ben, and so on, with the animal drawn in place of its name. The child reads the grid, decides whether each sentence is true, and circles the tick or the cross.
G2-345.p2: Reading a finished grid is a different skill from filling one, and it is the skill that catches the child who fills grids by pattern without knowing what a tick means. A row with one tick and two crosses is a sentence in disguise, Tom has the tiger, and this page asks the child to translate it in both directions, including the negative form and the form that starts with the animal. Two or three of the five sentences are true on each grid, never all or none, so guessing does not work. The teacher looks at the does not have sentences, where a true statement is about a cross.
G2-345.p3: A one-sheet color print with no marks to make on the grids themselves. Use it before the base page with a child who is new to grids, or after it as the check that the marks were understood. The three clues, one answer page is the solving version, and the yes, no and either-or page adds clue kinds. Sentences to judge against a picture are the read and do family; here they are judged against a grid.
